passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 1
text: Kinase KinA transfers a phosphoryl group from ATP to a negatively charged phosphorylated sugar, substrate S. Researchers measured initial velocity (v) at several concentrations of S in the absence and presence of 20 µM compound I, a small molecule whose structure resembles S. ATP was kept at a saturating concentration, and the enzyme concentration was identical in all assays. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

In a separate experiment, a variant of KinA in which one active-site lysine was changed to alanine (K to A) bound S with markedly lower affinity than wild-type KinA. ATP binding and the maximum velocity measured at very high S were not noticeably altered by the substitution. Structural modeling indicated that the lysine side chain lies close to the carbon-6 phosphate group of S when S is bound.
The researchers concluded that compound I binds reversibly to the same site as S. They plan to use the inhibition constant (Ki) to compare compound I with related inhibitors.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 are most consistent with compound I acting as which type of inhibitor?
o: Noncompetitive, because the velocity is lower at every [S]
lower velocity at every [S] occurs in all inhibition types; noncompetitive inhibition would also lower Vₘₐₓ, which is not seen
Uncompetitive, because both the apparent Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ decrease
uncompetitive inhibition lowers both Kₘ and Vₘₐₓ; here Kₘ rises and Vₘₐₓ is unchanged
Competitive, because Vₘₐₓ is unchanged while the apparent Kₘ increases

Correct: With inhibitor, v approaches the same ceiling (about 100 µmol/min) at high [S] while the [S] needed for half-maximal velocity rises from 2 mM to about 6 mM, the signature of competitive inhibition.
Mixed, because the inhibitor binds both free enzyme and enzyme-substrate complex
mixed inhibition lowers Vₘₐₓ; Vₘₐₓ here is unchanged
qs.x: With inhibitor, v approaches the same ceiling (about 100 µmol/min) at high [S] while the [S] needed for half-maximal velocity rises from 2 mM to about 6 mM, the signature of competitive inhibition. Trap: Seeing lower velocity at each [S] and concluding Vₘₐₓ fell, when the curves are actually converging toward the same Vₘₐₓ at high [S].

qs.q: Using the data in Table 1, what is the approximate Ki of compound I?
o: 5 µM
would require Kₘ,app/Kₘ to equal 5, not 3
20 µM
this equals [I] and would double Kₘ rather than triple it
40 µM
this would give Kₘ,app/Kₘ of 1.5
10 µM
Correct: Control Kₘ is 2 mM and apparent Kₘ with inhibitor is 6 mM (v = 25 at 2 mM is half of 50, and Vₘₐₓ is about 100). Kₘ,app = Kₘ(1 + [I]/Ki), so 3 = 1 + 20/Ki and Ki = 10 µM.
qs.x: Control Kₘ is 2 mM and apparent Kₘ with inhibitor is 6 mM (v = 25 at 2 mM is half of 50, and Vₘₐₓ is about 100). Kₘ,app = Kₘ(1 + [I]/Ki), so 3 = 1 + 20/Ki and Ki = 10 µM. Trap: Setting Kₘ,app/Kₘ equal to [I]/Ki and forgetting the 1 in (1 + [I]/Ki).

qs.q: Assuming the same Kₘ,app and Vₘₐₓ, what is the approximate velocity with compound I present at [S] = 60 mM?
o: 91 µmol/min
Correct: v = Vₘₐₓ[S]/(Kₘ,app + [S]) = 100(60)/(6 + 60) = about 91 µmol/min; high substrate outcompetes a competitive inhibitor but does not fully reach Vₘₐₓ.
60 µmol/min
this would be the velocity near [S] = 9 mM, far lower than at 60 mM
75 µmol/min
this corresponds to [S] near 18 mM
100 µmol/min
Vₘₐₓ is approached but never reached at finite [S]
qs.x: v = Vₘₐₓ[S]/(Kₘ,app + [S]) = 100(60)/(6 + 60) = about 91 µmol/min; high substrate outcompetes a competitive inhibitor but does not fully reach Vₘₐₓ. Trap: Assuming a competitive inhibitor is completely overcome so that v equals Vₘₐₓ at any large [S].

qs.q: How would a Lineweaver-Burk (double-reciprocal) plot of the inhibited data compare with the uninhibited data?
o: Same x-intercept, steeper slope, and a larger y-intercept on the double-reciprocal plot
same x-intercept with different y-intercept describes noncompetitive inhibition
Parallel lines, with a larger y-intercept and an x-intercept closer to the origin
parallel lines describe uncompetitive inhibition
Same y-intercept, steeper slope, and an x-intercept closer to zero
Correct: The y-intercept (1/Vₘₐₓ) is unchanged and the x-intercept (−1/Kₘ,app) moves from −0.5 to about −0.17 mM⁻¹, so the slope Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ increases.
Same slope as the uninhibited line and a smaller y-intercept, indicating a higher Vₘₐₓ
a smaller y-intercept would mean higher Vₘₐₓ
qs.x: The y-intercept (1/Vₘₐₓ) is unchanged and the x-intercept (−1/Kₘ,app) moves from −0.5 to about −0.17 mM⁻¹, so the slope Kₘ/Vₘₐₓ increases. Trap: Remembering the intercepts of the wrong inhibition type (noncompetitive shifts the y-intercept, competitive does not).

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the K to A variant bound S poorly?
o: The lysine side chain normally forms a disulfide bond with S
disulfide bonds require cysteine residues, not lysine
Lysine contributes a hydrophobic surface that buries the sugar ring of S
lysine is long and charged, not hydrophobic, and S binding rather than burial is at issue
The protonated lysine side chain normally forms an ionic interaction with the negatively charged phosphate of S
Correct: At physiological pH the lysine amine is protonated and positively charged, so it can form a salt bridge with the phosphate; alanine is nonpolar and cannot.
Lysine normally forms a covalent bond with the phosphate of ATP
ATP binding was unaffected, so lysine is not needed for ATP interactions
qs.x: At physiological pH the lysine amine is protonated and positively charged, so it can form a salt bridge with the phosphate; alanine is nonpolar and cannot. Trap: Assuming the side chain acts through hydrophobic or covalent effects instead of using its charge at pH 7.4.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 2
text: MicroRNAs are approximately 22-nucleotide RNAs that regulate gene expression after transcription. Researchers studied miR-X, which has partial complementarity to a seven-nucleotide site in the 3' untranslated region (3' UTR) of the mRNA for gene G.

Cultured cells were treated in one of three ways: (1) a synthetic miR-X mimic was introduced; (2) an anti-miR-X oligonucleotide, which is perfectly complementary to miR-X and sequesters it, was introduced; or (3) cells expressing a version of gene G with the miR-X binding site in the 3' UTR mutated were given the miR-X mimic. After 48 hours, mRNA for G was measured by reverse transcription followed by quantitative PCR (RT-qPCR), and protein G was measured by Western blot. Both measurements were normalized to control genes and then expressed relative to untreated cells, which were set to 1.00. Results are shown in Table 1.
The researchers noted that the miR-X mimic had no effect on the abundance of the mRNA for an unrelated gene lacking the binding site.

qs.q: Which mechanism best explains the effect of the miR-X mimic on gene G?
o: miR-X binds the promoter of gene G in the nucleus and prevents RNA polymerase II from initiating transcription
microRNAs act on the mRNA, not promoter DNA, and transcription inhibition would not need a 3' UTR site
miR-X enters the nucleus and base-pairs with the pre-mRNA of gene G, blocking splicing of its exons before export
splicing does not involve the 3' UTR site tested and the effect was lost when the UTR site was mutated
miR-X binds protein G after translation and tags it with ubiquitin, targeting it for degradation by the proteasome in the cytosol
miR-X pairs with RNA, not protein
miR-X, within a silencing complex, base-pairs imperfectly with the 3' UTR to reduce translation and promote mRNA decay
Correct: The mimic lowered both mRNA and protein (protein more), as expected for a microRNA that represses translation and destabilizes mRNA through partial pairing with the 3' UTR.
qs.x: The mimic lowered both mRNA and protein (protein more), as expected for a microRNA that represses translation and destabilizes mRNA through partial pairing with the 3' UTR. Trap: Choosing a transcriptional mechanism because mRNA fell, ignoring that the effect depends on a 3' UTR sequence.

qs.q: What is the most valid conclusion from the mutated-site condition?
o: The mimic cannot enter cells expressing the mutated gene, so no repression is seen
the same mimic was delivered, and no data address uptake
miR-X reduces expression of all genes equally, regardless of sequence match
an unrelated gene was unaffected, so repression is gene-specific
Repression of G by the mimic depends on the miR-X site in the 3' UTR
Correct: Mutating only the binding site abolished the mimic's effect (0.98 and 0.95 versus 0.45 and 0.20), showing sequence-specific dependence.
Translation of G does not require the 3' UTR, so the mutation is irrelevant
the experiment tests the binding site, not the general role of the UTR in translation
qs.x: Mutating only the binding site abolished the mimic's effect (0.98 and 0.95 versus 0.45 and 0.20), showing sequence-specific dependence. Trap: Overgeneralizing from one condition to claims that the data do not test.

qs.q: The anti-miR-X condition increased protein G to 1.50. This result suggests that:
o: endogenous miR-X normally represses gene G in these cells
Correct: Removing endogenous miR-X by sequestration relieved repression, so protein rose above the untreated baseline.
gene G is not a target of miR-X, so anti-miR-X should have no effect
a nonresponsive gene would show no change
miR-X increases transcription of gene G through its promoter in these cells
the mimic decreased expression, so miR-X is not a transcriptional activator
anti-miR-X is translated into additional protein G in these cells
anti-miR-X is an oligonucleotide with no relationship to the sequence of G
qs.x: Removing endogenous miR-X by sequestration relieved repression, so protein rose above the untreated baseline. Trap: Expecting no effect from an inhibitor because the cells were 'untreated' and assumed to lack the microRNA.

qs.q: Using Table 1, by approximately what percent did the miR-X mimic reduce protein produced per mRNA molecule?
o: 0.20 is the relative protein, not a per-mRNA value
Correct: Protein per mRNA = 0.20/0.45 = 0.44 of baseline, a decrease of 56%.
0.44 is the remaining fraction rather than the reduction
80% is the total protein reduction and ignores that mRNA also fell
qs.x: Protein per mRNA = 0.20/0.45 = 0.44 of baseline, a decrease of 56%. Trap: Using protein level alone and forgetting that fewer mRNA molecules were also present.

qs.q: Why must RNA be converted to complementary DNA before the qPCR step used to measure mRNA of gene G?
o: The DNA polymerase used in PCR requires a DNA template
Correct: Reverse transcriptase makes cDNA from the RNA template; thermostable DNA polymerase then amplifies it.
Introns must be removed from mRNA before amplification
mature mRNA has already been spliced
The 5' cap must be added to mRNA for primers to bind
caps are irrelevant to primer annealing in cDNA
The mRNA must be degraded to remove genomic DNA contamination
reverse transcription does not degrade genomic DNA
qs.x: Reverse transcriptase makes cDNA from the RNA template; thermostable DNA polymerase then amplifies it. Trap: Believing reverse transcription performs RNA processing steps such as splicing.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 3
text: A rare autosomal recessive metabolic disorder results from homozygosity for a loss-of-function allele (a) of a single gene. Heterozygous carriers (Aa) are healthy. Public health researchers genotyped random samples from two geographic regions and counted affected individuals (genotype aa). Results are shown in Table 1.

For analysis, the researchers assumed that each region was in Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium for this gene, with p representing the frequency of the dominant allele (A) and q representing the frequency of allele a. They also assumed that affected individuals were identified without error and that the allele has no effect on survival before reproduction in either region.

In follow-up interviews, the researchers learned that marriage between relatives is more common in Region B than in Region A. They plan to compare observed genotype frequencies with Hardy-Weinberg expectations in a larger study. Both regions have similar age distributions, and migration between the regions is negligible, so differences in allele frequency are attributed to local population history.

qs.q: What is the frequency of allele a in Region A?
o: 0.0004 is q², the frequency of affected individuals
0.04 is the value for Region B
0.20 would give q² = 0.04
qs.x: q² = 4/10,000 = 0.0004, so q = 0.02. Trap: Reporting q² as the allele frequency without taking the square root.

qs.q: What is the expected carrier frequency in Region B?
o: 0.16% is the affected frequency
4% is q, ignoring the factor of 2p
16% would result from doubling q incorrectly twice
qs.x: q² = 16/10,000 = 0.0016, so q = 0.04 and p = 0.96. Carriers = 2pq = 2(0.96)(0.04) = 0.0768, about 7.7%. Trap: Using q or 2q as the carrier frequency instead of 2pq.

qs.q: A healthy person in either region has an affected sibling, and both parents are unaffected. What is the probability that the healthy person is a carrier?
o: Correct: Both parents must be Aa. Among unaffected offspring the genotypes are AA (1/4) and Aa (1/2), so the carrier probability is (1/2)/(3/4) = 2/3.
1/4 is the chance of an affected child
1/2 ignores that the person is known to be unaffected
3/4 is the chance of being unaffected
qs.x: Both parents must be Aa. Among unaffected offspring the genotypes are AA (1/4) and Aa (1/2), so the carrier probability is (1/2)/(3/4) = 2/3. Trap: Failing to restrict the sample space to unaffected offspring.

qs.q: Which factor would most likely cause the observed frequency of affected individuals in Region B to exceed the Hardy-Weinberg expectation based on its allele frequency?
o: Random mating among all individuals, so genotype frequencies match p², 2pq, and q² expectations
random mating is an HW assumption and would match expectation
Mating among relatives, raising homozygosity without changing allele frequency
Correct: Inbreeding increases the proportion of homozygotes (aa) relative to HW predictions while leaving q unchanged.
A very large population size, which minimizes random changes in allele frequency by drift
large population size limits drift and is an HW assumption
Absence of mutation and migration, so no new alleles enter or leave the gene pool
no mutation or migration is an HW assumption
qs.x: Inbreeding increases the proportion of homozygotes (aa) relative to HW predictions while leaving q unchanged. Trap: Confusing a violated Hardy-Weinberg assumption with one that is actually met.

qs.q: About how many carriers are expected among the 10,000 people genotyped in Region A?
o: 39 is a factor of 10 too small
196 is half of the carrier count
980 corresponds to a carrier frequency of 9.8%, far above 2pq = 3.9%, and has no basis in the calculation
qs.x: q = 0.02 and p = 0.98, so 2pq = 0.0392 and 0.0392 × 10,000 = 392. Trap: Dropping the factor of 2 when computing the heterozygote frequency.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 4
text: Researchers measured the oxygen consumption rate (OCR) of cultured cells in a sealed microplate with an oxygen sensor. After baseline measurements, compounds were injected sequentially at the times indicated and OCR was measured every 10 minutes. Oligomycin inhibits ATP synthase. FCCP is a lipid-soluble weak acid that carries protons across membranes. A mixture of rotenone, which inhibits Complex I, and antimycin A, which inhibits Complex III, was used at the end of the experiment. Cells were supplied with glucose and other nutrients throughout.

Mean OCR values are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1. Oligomycin was added after the 20-minute measurement, FCCP after the 40-minute measurement, and rotenone with antimycin A after the 60-minute measurement. The researchers attributed the OCR remaining after the final injection to oxygen-consuming reactions outside the mitochondrial electron transport chain.

The researchers used the values to estimate ATP-linked respiration, proton leak, and spare respiratory capacity. Spare respiratory capacity is the difference between the maximal OCR and the basal OCR.

qs.q: Why does OCR fall after oligomycin is added?
o: Oligomycin directly inhibits Complex IV, preventing the transfer of electrons to oxygen
Complex IV is not the target of oligomycin
Oligomycin depletes NADH by blocking glycolysis upstream of the citric acid cycle
glycolysis is not affected and NADH supply is not the limiting step
Blocking ATP synthase stops proton re-entry, so the gradient rises and slows electron transport
Correct: Without proton flow through ATP synthase, the proton-motive force builds and opposes further proton pumping, so oxygen use drops to the leak-driven rate.
Oligomycin makes the inner membrane freely permeable to protons, dissipating the gradient across the membrane
a permeable membrane (uncoupling) would increase OCR, as FCCP does
qs.x: Without proton flow through ATP synthase, the proton-motive force builds and opposes further proton pumping, so oxygen use drops to the leak-driven rate. Trap: Thinking that any inhibitor of oxidative phosphorylation must directly block the electron transport chain.

qs.q: Based on Table 1, what is the ATP-linked respiration in pmol O₂/min?
o: 30 equals 40 − 10, the proton leak
120 is the total basal OCR
140 is the spare capacity
Correct: ATP-linked OCR is the basal OCR minus the oligomycin-insensitive OCR: 120 − 40 = 80.
qs.x: ATP-linked OCR is the basal OCR minus the oligomycin-insensitive OCR: 120 − 40 = 80. Trap: Subtracting the final residual value (10) instead of the oligomycin value (40).

qs.q: Which statement best explains the increase in OCR after FCCP?
o: FCCP carries protons into the matrix, dissipating the gradient so electron transport runs unrestrained
Correct: Dissipating the proton gradient removes back-pressure on the electron transport chain, which then consumes oxygen at its maximal rate while producing heat instead of ATP.
FCCP activates ATP synthase to its maximal rate, which consumes the gradient faster than it forms
ATP synthase was already inhibited by oligomycin
FCCP donates electrons directly to oxygen, bypassing Complexes III and IV and raising consumption in the matrix
FCCP does not donate electrons
FCCP inhibits Complex I, relieving feedback inhibition on glycolysis and increasing NADH supply
inhibiting Complex I would reduce, not raise, OCR
qs.x: Dissipating the proton gradient removes back-pressure on the electron transport chain, which then consumes oxygen at its maximal rate while producing heat instead of ATP. Trap: Assuming that higher oxygen consumption must reflect more ATP synthesis.

qs.q: What is the spare respiratory capacity of the cells, in pmol O₂/min?
o: 80 is the ATP-linked OCR
Correct: Spare capacity = maximal OCR - basal OCR = 260 − 120 = 140.
130 is half the maximal OCR and has no basis in the calculation
260 is the maximal OCR itself
qs.x: Spare capacity = maximal OCR - basal OCR = 260 − 120 = 140. Trap: Reporting the maximal OCR rather than the difference from basal.

qs.q: If only rotenone were added to the cells, which substrate would most likely still support substantial oxygen consumption?
o: Pyruvate
pyruvate provides NADH via the matrix, requiring Complex I
Succinate
Correct: Succinate is oxidized by Complex II, which feeds electrons to ubiquinone downstream of Complex I.
Malate
malate is oxidized to produce NADH, requiring Complex I
Glutamate
glutamate yields NADH via dehydrogenases, requiring Complex I
qs.x: Succinate is oxidized by Complex II, which feeds electrons to ubiquinone downstream of Complex I. Trap: Overlooking that Complex II enters the chain below the rotenone block.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 5
text: Cytoskeletal elements were probed in cultured epithelial cells using drugs that target specific polymers. Colchicine binds tubulin dimers and prevents their polymerization. Cytochalasin D caps the plus ends of actin filaments and prevents their elongation. Paclitaxel binds microtubules and stabilizes them against depolymerization.

Cells were treated for 24 hours with each drug, fixed, and stained for DNA, keratin, and mitochondria. The percentage of cells in mitosis (condensed chromosomes with no nuclear envelope) and the percentage of cells with two nuclei were determined from at least 500 cells per condition. Mitochondrial distribution was assessed qualitatively. Keratin filament networks appeared intact under all conditions, and cells remained attached to the dish.

In colchicine-treated and paclitaxel-treated cells, most mitotic cells had chromosomes clustered near the cell center without a bipolar spindle (colchicine) or with abnormal multipolar spindles (paclitaxel). Results are summarized in Table 1. The investigators emphasized that all three drugs were used at concentrations that did not reduce cell viability over the treatment period, and that untreated cells were handled identically in every other respect.

qs.q: The increase in mitotic cells after colchicine is best explained by:
o: failure to replicate DNA in S phase, so cells cannot enter mitosis at all
cells with unreplicated DNA would stall in G1 or S, not in mitosis
loss of the contractile ring during telophase, which prevents separation of daughter cells
contractile-ring failure produces binucleate cells, not mitotic arrest
failure to assemble a spindle, which activates the spindle assembly checkpoint and blocks anaphase
Correct: Without microtubules chromosomes cannot attach and align, so the checkpoint holds cells in mitosis.
premature degradation of cyclin B, which would force cells out of mitosis too early
premature cyclin B loss would drive mitotic exit
qs.x: Without microtubules chromosomes cannot attach and align, so the checkpoint holds cells in mitosis. Trap: Assigning the arrest to the wrong cell-cycle stage because the drug is called an antimitotic.

qs.q: The binucleate cells seen after cytochalasin D most likely arise because:
o: the actin-myosin contractile ring cannot form, so cytokinesis fails after nuclear division
Correct: Mitosis proceeds (mitotic index is normal), but without functional actin the cleavage furrow does not form.
chromosomes cannot attach to spindle microtubules, so mitosis stalls before anaphase
spindle attachment depends on microtubules, which this drug does not target
DNA replication occurs twice per cycle, producing nuclei with doubled DNA content
re-replication would not produce two normal nuclei in this way
the nuclear envelope fails to reassemble, leaving chromosomes exposed to the cytoplasm after each division
nuclear envelope reformation is lamin-dependent and unaffected here
qs.x: Mitosis proceeds (mitotic index is normal), but without functional actin the cleavage furrow does not form. Trap: Confusing karyokinesis (division of the nucleus) with cytokinesis (division of the cytoplasm).

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for perinuclear clustering of mitochondria after colchicine?
o: Colchicine disrupts keratin filaments that anchor mitochondria near the cell center
keratin was intact under all conditions
Loss of microtubule tracks prevents kinesin-driven transport toward the cell periphery
Correct: Kinesins carry mitochondria outward along microtubules; without them, cargo drifts toward the center.
Dynein can only move cargo toward the plus end of microtubules, away from the nucleus, so mitochondria cannot reach the periphery
dynein moves toward the minus end, near the centrosome, not the plus end
Colchicine causes mitochondria to fuse with the nuclear envelope near the centrosome
no data support fusion with the nucleus
qs.x: Kinesins carry mitochondria outward along microtubules; without them, cargo drifts toward the center. Trap: Reversing the polarity of motor protein movement (kinesin: plus end; dynein: minus end).

qs.q: Why would paclitaxel, which stabilizes microtubules, also increase the fraction of cells in mitosis?
o: Stable microtubules prevent chromosomes from condensing during prophase and prometaphase
chromosomes did condense in mitotic cells
Dynamic microtubule shortening is required for proper chromosome movement and spindle function
Correct: Spindle assembly and chromosome segregation require polymerization and depolymerization, so overly stable microtubules give abnormal spindles and checkpoint arrest.
Stabilized microtubules inhibit actin polymerization directly, blocking the cleavage furrow and halting mitosis
no data suggest a direct effect on actin
Paclitaxel prevents cells from entering S phase, so they never reach the spindle stage
entry into S phase is not blocked, as cells reach mitosis
qs.x: Spindle assembly and chromosome segregation require polymerization and depolymerization, so overly stable microtubules give abnormal spindles and checkpoint arrest. Trap: Assuming that stabilizing a polymer is the opposite of disrupting it and therefore harmless to mitosis.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 6
text: A clinical laboratory found that a drug-resistant bacterial strain could pass resistance to a susceptible strain. Researchers hypothesized that resistance was encoded on a plasmid that is transferred between cells. A donor strain carrying the resistance plasmid was mixed with a susceptible recipient strain and incubated for 1 hour. Mixtures were then plated on medium containing the antibiotic and a nutrient supplement that allowed only recipients to grow, and the number of resistant recipient colonies (transconjugants) per donor cell was calculated.

Four conditions were tested. In condition 1, donor and recipient cells were mixed. In condition 2, the mixture was incubated with DNase I, which degrades DNA outside cells. In condition 3, donor and recipient were separated by a filter with 0.2 µm pores in a U-shaped tube, allowing the medium, but not cells, to pass; bacteriophage particles (about 0.05 µm) can pass through the filter. In condition 4, the donor carried a mutation that prevents production of a pilus. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

qs.q: Which conclusion about the transfer mechanism is best supported by condition 2?
o: Transfer requires DNase I to cleave the plasmid before it enters the recipient
transfer persisted without a decrease, not needing DNase I
Transfer is carried out by bacteriophage particles that package the plasmid
phage involvement is addressed by the filter condition
DNase I inhibits the recipient's growth, which lowers the number of colonies counted in the DNase-treated sample
a growth defect would lower colony counts, which did not occur
Transfer does not require free DNA in the medium, which argues against transformation
Correct: DNase would have destroyed extracellular DNA; transfer remained at 1.1 × 10⁻³, so naked DNA uptake is not the mechanism.
qs.x: DNase would have destroyed extracellular DNA; transfer remained at 1.1 × 10⁻³, so naked DNA uptake is not the mechanism. Trap: Taking an unchanged result as meaningless instead of as evidence that excludes a mechanism.

qs.q: The results of condition 3 are best interpreted as indicating that:
o: transfer requires a soluble signal molecule secreted by the donor cells into the medium and acts across the filter
a soluble signal would have crossed the filter
the filter blocks plasmid DNA but not whole cells, so contact is not needed
the filter blocks cells, not DNA, and free DNA was not the mechanism
direct cell-to-cell contact is required, which also excludes phage-mediated transduction
Correct: Medium and phage particles can cross the filter but no transfer occurred, so contact is needed and transduction is excluded.
phage particles carry the plasmid across the filter and infect the recipient cells
phages pass the filter, yet transfer fell below detection
qs.x: Medium and phage particles can cross the filter but no transfer occurred, so contact is needed and transduction is excluded. Trap: Forgetting that phage particles are small enough to cross the filter.

qs.q: Which description of the transfer in condition 1 is most accurate?
o: One plasmid strand is nicked and transferred through the pilus junction, then each cell makes a complementary strand
Correct: Conjugation involves single-strand transfer with replication in both cells, so the donor keeps its plasmid.
Both strands of the plasmid are transferred through the pilus and the donor loses the plasmid permanently, ending the transfer
the donor retains the plasmid, which supports the donor-to-recipient copies
The plasmid is transferred as a double-stranded linear molecule packaged within a phage protein coat
a phage coat is not involved
The plasmid is integrated into the recipient chromosome by a viral integrase after uptake of free DNA
integration by viral integrase describes retroviruses
qs.x: Conjugation involves single-strand transfer with replication in both cells, so the donor keeps its plasmid. Trap: Assuming the donor loses its plasmid, as if the DNA were moved rather than copied.

qs.q: If 5 × 10⁷ donor cells were used in condition 1, about how many transconjugants would be expected?
o: this is off by a factor of 10
Correct: (1.2 × 10⁻³ per donor)(5 × 10⁷ donors) = 6 × 10⁴.
this results from dividing 5 × 10⁷ by the frequency
this results from dividing the frequency by the number of donors (1.2 × 10⁻³ / 5 × 10⁷ = 2 × 10⁻¹¹)
qs.x: (1.2 × 10⁻³ per donor)(5 × 10⁷ donors) = 6 × 10⁴. Trap: Dividing instead of multiplying when converting a per-donor frequency to a total count.

graph.x_label: Condition (1 = mixed, 2 = mixed + DNase I, 3 = filter-separated, 4 = pilus-deficient donor)

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 7
text: Researchers studied two investigational compounds, Drug X and Drug Y, in a proliferating human cell line with a doubling time of 24 hours. Cells were treated for 24 hours, fixed, stained with a fluorescent dye that binds DNA stoichiometrically, and analyzed by flow cytometry. Cells with a diploid (2N) DNA content were classified as G1, cells with intermediate DNA content as S, and cells with 4N DNA content as G2/M. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

Untreated cells were asynchronous, and the researchers assumed that the fraction of cells in each phase is proportional to the time spent in that phase. Western blots of treated cells indicated that Drug Y-treated cells contained hypophosphorylated retinoblastoma protein (Rb), while Drug X-treated cells showed many cells with condensed chromosomes and a few visible spindle fibers. Drug X had no detectable effect on DNA replication measured by incorporation of a labeled nucleotide.

qs.q: The Drug Y results are most consistent with inhibition of:
o: the spindle assembly checkpoint
inhibiting the spindle checkpoint would not cause G1 accumulation
G1 cyclin-dependent kinase activity that normally phosphorylates Rb
Correct: Hypophosphorylated Rb holds E2F in an inactive state, so cells cannot enter S phase and accumulate in G1.
DNA polymerase during S phase
inhibition of DNA polymerase would increase the S fraction
cyclin B-CDK1 activity at the G2/M transition
inhibition of cyclin B-CDK1 would increase G2/M cells
qs.x: Hypophosphorylated Rb holds E2F in an inactive state, so cells cannot enter S phase and accumulate in G1. Trap: Matching the drug to the phase where cells accumulate before considering which phase the compound acts to prevent entering.

qs.q: Which process is Drug X most likely to interfere with?
o: Initiation of DNA replication at origins
replication was unaffected and a block would lower S-phase entry rather than raise G2/M
Assembly or function of the mitotic spindle
Correct: Cells with replicated DNA, condensed chromosomes, and few spindle fibers that accumulate at 4N DNA content suggest a mitotic block, and replication was unaffected.
Phosphorylation of Rb by G1 cyclin-CDK complexes
Rb phosphorylation is the G1 step affected by Drug Y
Synthesis of histones during G1
histone synthesis defects would affect S phase, not mitosis
qs.x: Cells with replicated DNA, condensed chromosomes, and few spindle fibers that accumulate at 4N DNA content suggest a mitotic block, and replication was unaffected. Trap: Assuming a 4N accumulation must reflect a defect in DNA synthesis.

qs.q: Under the assumptions stated, how long does S phase last in untreated cells?
o: 3.6 hours
3.6 hours corresponds to 15%, the G2/M fraction
7.2 hours
Correct: 0.30 × 24 hours = 7.2 hours.
13.2 hours
13.2 hours corresponds to 55%, the G1 fraction
30 hours
30 is the percentage, not a time
qs.x: 0.30 × 24 hours = 7.2 hours. Trap: Using the percentage value as hours, or the percentage of the wrong phase.

qs.q: How many chromatids are present in a human cell in G2?
o: 23 is the haploid number
46 is the chromosome count and the chromatid count in G1 is also 46 as each chromosome has one chromatid
184 doubles 92 incorrectly
Correct: Human cells have 46 chromosomes; after S phase each consists of two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids.
qs.x: Human cells have 46 chromosomes; after S phase each consists of two sister chromatids, giving 92 chromatids. Trap: Confusing chromosome number with chromatid number after replication.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 8
text: Researchers compared glucose handling in control mice and in mice carrying a liver-specific mutation in a gene required for insulin receptor signaling. After a 6-hour fast, each mouse received an intraperitoneal injection of glucose, and blood samples were collected at the times shown. Blood glucose was measured with a meter and plasma insulin with an immunoassay. Each value is the mean of 8 mice. Results are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

Fasting body weights were similar in the two groups. Pancreatic islets isolated from mutant mice and control mice secreted similar amounts of insulin when exposed to the same glucose concentrations in vitro. The researchers also measured liver glycogen content after the fast, finding lower glycogen in the mutant livers.
The investigators interpreted the data as evidence that the mutation produces a state resembling the early stage of type 2 diabetes. They then planned a second study of glucagon during a longer fast.

qs.q: The data in Table 1 are best interpreted as showing that mutant mice have:
o: insulin deficiency caused by impaired islet function
insulin levels were higher, not lower, and islets function normally in vitro
enhanced insulin sensitivity in peripheral tissue
greater sensitivity would lower glucose clearance time, not lengthen it
reduced insulin sensitivity, with compensatory elevated insulin secretion
Correct: Mutant mice have higher glucose and higher insulin than controls; islets secrete normally in vitro, so tissues respond poorly to insulin.
excess glucagon secretion that lowers blood glucose
glucagon raises blood glucose and is not suggested to lower it
qs.x: Mutant mice have higher glucose and higher insulin than controls; islets secrete normally in vitro, so tissues respond poorly to insulin. Trap: Equating high glucose with low insulin; here insulin was high, indicating resistance rather than deficiency.

qs.q: Which sequence best describes how glucose entry stimulates insulin release from pancreatic β cells?
o: Increased ATP/ADP closes K⁺ channels, causing depolarization, Ca²⁺ entry, and exocytosis of insulin
Correct: Glucose metabolism raises ATP, closing ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels; depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion.
Increased cAMP opens Na⁺ channels, causing hyperpolarization and insulin degradation
cAMP and Na⁺ channel opening are not the glucose-sensing pathway, and the cell is depolarized rather than hyperpolarized
Decreased ATP opens K⁺ channels, causing depolarization and Ca²⁺ release
a decrease in ATP would keep K⁺ channels open and prevent depolarization
Glucose binds a receptor tyrosine kinase that directly triggers vesicle fusion
the insulin receptor responds to insulin on target cells, not to glucose on β cells
qs.x: Glucose metabolism raises ATP, closing ATP-sensitive K⁺ channels; depolarization opens voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels and Ca²⁺ triggers vesicle fusion. Trap: Reversing the effect of ATP on the K-ATP channel.

qs.q: By approximately what percent did mutant blood glucose at 120 minutes exceed its fasting value?
o: 47% divides the change by 180 instead of 95
53% divides the baseline by the final value (95/180)
189% is the ratio 180/95 and not the increase
qs.x: (180 − 95)/95 = 0.895, about 89%. Trap: Reporting the ratio to baseline as the percent increase.

qs.q: During a prolonged fast, glucagon from pancreatic α cells would be expected to:
o: lower blood glucose by stimulating glycogen synthesis in liver and glucose uptake in muscle
glycogen synthesis is promoted by insulin
raise blood glucose by stimulating glucose uptake and triglyceride storage in adipose tissue
glucose uptake in adipose tissue is insulin-dependent and would lower glucose
raise blood glucose by stimulating hepatic glycogen breakdown and gluconeogenesis via cAMP
Correct: Glucagon activates a G protein-coupled receptor on hepatocytes, raising cAMP and activating PKA, which promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis.
lower blood glucose by inhibiting gluconeogenesis through insulin receptors on hepatocytes
glucagon does not act through insulin receptors
qs.x: Glucagon activates a G protein-coupled receptor on hepatocytes, raising cAMP and activating PKA, which promotes glycogenolysis and gluconeogenesis. Trap: Assigning glucagon's role to that of insulin.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 9
text: To characterize renal handling of several solutes, researchers infused inulin, a polysaccharide that is freely filtered and neither reabsorbed nor secreted, into a healthy volunteer. Timed urine was collected for one hour and a mid-collection blood sample was obtained. Plasma and urine concentrations of inulin, glucose, urea, and a drug (substance X) were measured. Urine flow was constant at 1.0 mL/min.
Substance X is not bound to plasma proteins and is known to be a substrate for an organic anion transporter in the proximal tubule. Results are shown in Table 1.

Clearance of a substance equals its urine concentration times urine flow, divided by its plasma concentration. The researchers compared the clearance of each substance with the glomerular filtration rate (GFR), which is equal to the clearance of inulin. They also compared the filtered load of each solute (GFR times plasma concentration) with the amount excreted (urine concentration times urine flow). Finally, they asked how changes in antidiuretic hormone (ADH) would alter the urinary concentrations.

qs.q: What is the GFR of the volunteer?
o: 31 mL/min
31 results from dividing by 2 twice
62.5 mL/min
62.5 ignores the division by plasma concentration
125 mL/min
Correct: Inulin clearance = (62.5 mg/mL x 1.0 mL/min)/0.50 mg/mL = 125 mL/min.
180 mL/min
180 is the typical daily filtrate volume in liters per day, not a rate in mL/min
qs.x: Inulin clearance = (62.5 mg/mL x 1.0 mL/min)/0.50 mg/mL = 125 mL/min. Trap: Forgetting to divide by the plasma concentration.

qs.q: Which conclusion about substance X is best supported by the data?
o: It is reabsorbed, because its clearance is below the GFR
clearance is above, not below, the GFR
It is neither filtered nor secreted
excretion above the filtered amount cannot occur without secretion
It undergoes net tubular secretion, because its clearance exceeds the GFR
Correct: Clearance of X = (30 × 1.0)/0.20 = 150 mL/min, which is greater than 125 mL/min, so more is excreted than filtered; transporters in the proximal tubule add it to the filtrate.
It is freely filtered and not reabsorbed or secreted
a freely filtered, unprocessed solute has a clearance equal to GFR
qs.x: Clearance of X = (30 × 1.0)/0.20 = 150 mL/min, which is greater than 125 mL/min, so more is excreted than filtered; transporters in the proximal tubule add it to the filtrate. Trap: Comparing concentrations rather than clearances.

qs.q: How much urea is reabsorbed per minute?
o: 15 mg/min
15 mg/min is the excreted amount
22.5 mg/min
Correct: Filtered = 125 mL/min x 0.30 mg/mL = 37.5 mg/min. Excreted = 15 mg/min. Reabsorbed = 37.5 − 15 = 22.5 mg/min.
37.5 mg/min
37.5 mg/min is the filtered amount
52.5 mg/min
52.5 mg/min adds excretion to filtered load
qs.x: Filtered = 125 mL/min x 0.30 mg/mL = 37.5 mg/min. Excreted = 15 mg/min. Reabsorbed = 37.5 − 15 = 22.5 mg/min. Trap: Reporting excreted or filtered amounts instead of their difference.

qs.q: After water deprivation, urine flow falls to 0.5 mL/min with GFR unchanged and plasma inulin unchanged. What is the urine inulin concentration?
o: 125 mg/mL
Correct: Inulin excretion is fixed at GFR x P = 62.5 mg/min. Urine concentration = 62.5/0.5 = 125 mg/mL, as ADH increases collecting-duct water reabsorption.
31 mg/mL
31 mg/mL would be if flow had doubled
62.5 mg/mL
62.5 mg/mL is the original value and assumes no concentration
250 mg/mL
250 mg/mL doubles the correct value
qs.x: Inulin excretion is fixed at GFR x P = 62.5 mg/min. Urine concentration = 62.5/0.5 = 125 mg/mL, as ADH increases collecting-duct water reabsorption. Trap: Assuming urine concentration is unchanged when only flow changes.

passages.title: FL01 · Bio/Biochem · Passage 10
text: Voltage-clamp recordings were made from isolated squid giant axons to separate the ionic currents underlying the action potential. The membrane potential was stepped from −70 mV to 0 mV, and the peak early inward current and peak late outward current were measured. Inward current is negative and outward current is positive.

In control conditions the axon was bathed in normal artificial seawater. Tetrodotoxin (TTX), a toxin that blocks the pore of one class of voltage-gated channel, was added in the second condition. In the third condition, tetraethylammonium (TEA) was injected into the axon. In the fourth condition, the extracellular Na⁺ concentration was lowered to 30% of normal with choline replacing Na⁺. Each condition was tested on a different axon, and each value is the mean of five axons. Results are shown in Table 1.

In current-clamp experiments on separate axons, application of TEA made the action potentials longer in duration without changing their threshold. The researchers also compared conduction in myelinated and unmyelinated axons from a vertebrate nerve.

qs.q: The effect of TTX on the currents indicates that TTX blocks:
o: voltage-gated K⁺ channels
K⁺ channel block would reduce the outward current, as TEA does
Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase
the pump is not voltage-gated and does not generate this fast current
voltage-gated Ca²⁺ channels
Ca²⁺ channels were not tested and the inward current vanished completely
voltage-gated Na⁺ channels
Correct: TTX abolished the early inward current but left the outward current intact, identifying the Na⁺ current.
qs.x: TTX abolished the early inward current but left the outward current intact, identifying the Na⁺ current. Trap: Identifying TTX with K⁺ channels because the outward current is easier to see.

qs.q: Why is the peak inward current smaller in low extracellular Na⁺?
o: Na⁺ channels are inactivated by choline, which reduces the peak inward current and blocks inward current
no data suggest choline inactivates channels, and outward current was unchanged
The Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase reverses its direction and pumps Na⁺ into the axon
the pump's direction does not reverse
K⁺ efflux increases enough to cancel the Na⁺ current at the 0 mV step
the outward current did not change
The Na⁺ equilibrium potential becomes less positive, reducing the driving force for Na⁺ entry
Correct: By the Nernst equation, lowering [Na⁺]out lowers E_Na, so at 0 mV the electrochemical gradient favoring Na⁺ entry shrinks.
qs.x: By the Nernst equation, lowering [Na⁺]out lowers E_Na, so at 0 mV the electrochemical gradient favoring Na⁺ entry shrinks. Trap: Assuming that channel number, not driving force, must be changed when current falls.

qs.q: How does TEA most likely lengthen the action potential?
o: By blocking Na⁺ channels, it raises the threshold
Na⁺ block would abolish action potentials and the inward current was unchanged
By opening Na⁺ channels, it slows inactivation
the inward current was not enhanced
By increasing the Na⁺/K⁺ ATPase rate, it hyperpolarizes the membrane
the pump contributes little to repolarization on the timescale of one action potential
By blocking K⁺ channels, it slows repolarization
Correct: TEA reduced the late outward K⁺ current (+2.0 to +0.3 nA), so the repolarizing current falls and the action potential broadens.
qs.x: TEA reduced the late outward K⁺ current (+2.0 to +0.3 nA), so the repolarizing current falls and the action potential broadens. Trap: Linking a longer action potential to Na⁺ channels because Na⁺ drives depolarization.

qs.q: Compared with unmyelinated axons of equal diameter, myelinated axons conduct faster mainly because:
o: myelin increases the number of open Na⁺ channels along the internode
channels are concentrated at the nodes and sparse under myelin
myelin pumps Na⁺ out of the axon rapidly
myelin is an insulator and does not pump ions
action potentials regenerate only at nodes of Ranvier, and current flows passively between nodes
Correct: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so depolarization spreads passively to the next node, where voltage-gated channels are concentrated (saltatory conduction).
myelin lowers the resting potential to the threshold
a resting potential at threshold would produce spontaneous firing
qs.x: Myelin raises membrane resistance and lowers capacitance, so depolarization spreads passively to the next node, where voltage-gated channels are concentrated (saltatory conduction). Trap: Thinking myelin speeds conduction by acting on ion channels along the whole axon.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 1
text: Translators have long been described as traitors, and the accusation rests on an assumption so familiar that it rarely receives scrutiny: that a text possesses a stable core of meaning that exists prior to any language, and that the translator's task is to carry this core across a border without spilling any of it. On this view, a good translation is a transparent window and a bad one is a smudged pane. The metaphor is attractive because it flatters the original, but it conceals more than it reveals.

Consider what a translator of a nineteenth-century novel actually confronts. A sentence may be long, its subordinate clauses stacked like crates, while the target language may prefer short declaratives. To break the sentence is to alter the rhythm that gave the narrator an air of fussy deliberation; to preserve it is to produce English that no reader would call natural. Neither choice is neutral. Fidelity to syntax and fidelity to effect pull in opposite directions, and the translator must decide which to betray. The window metaphor has no place for such a decision, since a window does not choose.

Some theorists have responded by inverting the hierarchy, arguing that translation is a form of authorship and that the translated text is a new work that merely shares a lineage with its source. This position has the virtue of honesty about the translator's labor, but it overcorrects. A translator who feels free to rewrite the plot, relocate the setting, or silence a troublesome character is not exercising creative license so much as abandoning an obligation. Readers who pick up a translation extend a particular kind of trust: they assume that the book in their hands answers to another book, and that its departures, where they occur, are the price of conveying something rather than the product of whim.

A more defensible account treats translation as interpretation, comparable to a pianist's reading of a sonata. No one supposes that two performances of the same sonata must be identical in order for both to be faithful, yet no one supposes that any sequence of notes counts as a performance of it either. The score constrains without determining. Similarly, the source text sets limits, so that some renderings are simply wrong, while leaving a wide field of legitimate variation. Disagreement among translators then appears not as evidence of failure but as the natural consequence of a text rich enough to sustain more than one reading.

This account also explains a curious feature of literary history: translations age faster than originals. A novel written in 1850 may still read as lively prose, while its English version from 1890 strikes us as stiff and quaint. If translation merely transferred a fixed meaning, there would be no reason for the English version to date, since the meaning has not changed. But if a translation is an interpretation shaped by the idiom and expectations of its own moment, then it will inevitably carry the marks of that moment, and later readers will perceive them as the dust of an earlier age. The original, written within the living language, is dated only in the way that all older books are; the translation is dated twice.

None of this implies that retranslation is wasteful. Each generation of translators, by making different compromises, reveals aspects of the source that earlier versions obscured. The proliferation of versions is not a sign that the work has been lost in transit but that it continues to be found.

qs.q: Which of the following best expresses the main point of the passage?
o: Translators should be regarded as authors of new works whose obligations to the source are minimal.
The author calls this view an overcorrection.
Translation is better understood as a constrained act of interpretation than as the transfer of a fixed meaning between languages.
Correct: This captures the author's rejection of the window metaphor and endorsement of the pianist analogy.
Translations inevitably betray their originals, so retranslation is largely wasteful.
The author explicitly denies that retranslation is wasteful.
Nineteenth-century novels are especially hard to translate because of their long sentences.
The long sentence is only an illustration, not the point of the passage.
qs.x: This captures the author's rejection of the window metaphor and endorsement of the pianist analogy. Trap: Choosing the authorship view because it gets extended discussion; the author presents it as an overcorrection, not as the conclusion.

qs.q: The author discusses the long, subordinate-clause-heavy sentence primarily to show that
o: translators must choose between competing kinds of fidelity, a feature the window metaphor cannot represent.
Correct: The author ties the example to the claim that a window does not choose.
readers generally prefer natural-sounding translations to literal ones, so translators should always favor fluency over fidelity
The passage never reports reader preferences.
target languages generally prefer shorter sentences than source languages do, so long sentences are always broken up
The example is hypothetical and used to illustrate a choice, not a general rule about languages.
nineteenth-century prose is stylistically inferior to modern prose.
No evaluation of the novel's quality is offered.
qs.x: The author ties the example to the claim that a window does not choose. Trap: Turning an illustrative example into a general claim about languages instead of asking what point it serves in the argument.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the view that translation is a form of authorship is best described as
o: qualified approval, crediting one merit while rejecting its extreme conclusion.
Correct: The author praises its honesty about the translator's labor but says it overcorrects.
neutral indifference, since the author neither credits nor criticizes the view that translators are authors
The author takes a clear evaluative stance.
enthusiastic endorsement, treating translators as authors whose duties to the source text are minimal
The author says the view overcorrects and abandons an obligation.
dismissive contempt, treating the view as having no merit whatsoever for the understanding of translation
The author grants that the view has a virtue.
qs.x: The author praises its honesty about the translator's labor but says it overcorrects. Trap: Reading a sentence of praise as the author's overall position and ignoring the 'but it overcorrects' that follows.

qs.q: According to the passage, a translation is 'dated twice' because
o: translators of earlier eras were less skilled than modern translators, so their versions now seem clumsy and outdated
Skill is never discussed as a cause.
the source language changes faster than the target language, leaving the original harder to read with each decade
The passage makes no comparison of rates of linguistic change.
the meaning of the source text changes over time while the translation stays fixed in the words of its own period
The passage says the meaning has not changed.
it ages as an older book and also bears the idiom and expectations of the period in which it was made.
Correct: The passage gives exactly these two sources of datedness.
qs.x: The passage gives exactly these two sources of datedness. Trap: Supplying a plausible outside explanation (translator skill) rather than the one the passage actually states.

qs.q: Two respected translators render a poem very differently, but one mistakes a word meaning 'river bank' for one meaning 'financial institution.' Based on the passage, the author would most likely say that
o: both renderings are equally legitimate because disagreement among respected translators is natural and the source permits many readings
The author states that some renderings are simply wrong.
the stylistic difference is an error, but the mistaken word is acceptable creative license because translators are authors in their own right
This reverses the author's position.
the stylistic difference reflects legitimate variation, while the mistaken word falls outside the limits the source sets.
Correct: The author says the source constrains without determining, so some renderings are simply wrong.
both renderings fail because neither matches the original exactly, and no translation ever could
The author rejects exact transfer as the standard.
qs.x: The author says the source constrains without determining, so some renderings are simply wrong. Trap: Over-applying 'disagreement is natural' to every difference, forgetting the limits the source text still sets.

qs.q: The passage attributes which of the following assumptions to those who call translators traitors?
o: Readers who lack the source language cannot judge whether a translation is accurate, so they must simply trust the translator.
No claim about readers' judgment is attributed to the accusers.
A text has a meaning that exists independently of any language and can be carried over intact.
Correct: This is the 'stable core of meaning' in the first paragraph.
A translation should sound more natural to its readers than the original sounded to its first audience.
The passage says naturalness and fidelity can conflict, not that traitors want naturalness.
Translators generally lack sufficient knowledge of the source language to render its subtler meanings reliably.
Competence is never mentioned.
qs.x: This is the 'stable core of meaning' in the first paragraph. Trap: Picking a statement that sounds like a reason to call translators traitors without checking it against the passage's first paragraph.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 2
text: City planners have traditionally regarded street vending as a symptom of disorder, a residue of underdevelopment that modernization will eventually sweep away. Municipal codes in many cities reflect this assumption: vendors are licensed sparingly, confined to designated zones, or prohibited outright in commercial districts. Yet in cities around the world the number of street vendors has not declined as economies have grown; in several it has risen. This persistence is awkward for the view that vending is a transitional phenomenon, and it has prompted researchers to ask whether the planners' premise was mistaken from the start.

One line of argument holds that vending persists because it performs functions that formal retail does not. A vendor stationed outside a transit station sells to commuters at precisely the moment and place where demand peaks, in quantities as small as a single piece of fruit or a pair of batteries. Large stores cannot profitably serve such demand, because their costs of rent, staffing, and inventory presuppose bulk sales and steady foot traffic. The vendor's low overhead is not a defect of the enterprise but the source of its flexibility. Moreover, vending offers entry to people excluded from formal employment by lack of credentials, capital, or documentation. To close the street is therefore not simply to remove an eyesore; it is to remove a rung from a ladder that some residents have no other way of climbing.

Critics of vending respond that these virtues are purchased at a cost borne by others. Crowded sidewalks impede pedestrians, particularly those with disabilities; uninspected food poses health risks; and vendors who pay no taxes enjoy an advantage over shopkeepers who do. These objections deserve to be taken seriously, but they are not all of one kind. Some concern genuine harms, such as obstruction and contamination, which can in principle be addressed through regulation of where and how vending occurs. Others concern fairness among competitors, which might be addressed by bringing vendors into the tax system on terms they can afford. Only if one assumes that vending cannot be regulated, and can only be tolerated or eliminated, does the existence of these costs justify prohibition.

The experience of cities that have tried regulation is instructive but mixed. Where authorities have negotiated with vendor associations over designated spaces, standardized stalls, and modest fees, congestion has often fallen and complaints have diminished. But in other cities, formalization has produced fees and permit requirements that only the more established vendors could meet, driving the poorest out to operate illegally and thereby exposing them to harassment and confiscation. The lesson is not that regulation fails but that its design matters: rules written without the participation of those they govern tend to serve the interests of those who wrote them.

It would be a mistake, then, to treat the debate as a contest between order and chaos. The street is a shared resource whose uses compete, and every arrangement of it, including the arrangement that excludes vendors, embodies a judgment about whose needs count. Planners who recognize this are better placed to ask which combination of rules would allow pedestrians, shopkeepers, and vendors to coexist, rather than assuming that one of the three is an intruder.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Vendors' advantages over shopkeepers, such as lower rent and exemption from taxes, are unfair enough to justify prohibiting street vending outright.
The author says fairness concerns can be addressed by other means.
Street vending persists for reasons planners overlooked, so the productive question is how to design fair regulations rather than whether to eliminate it.
Correct: This combines the persistence argument with the closing call for well-designed rules.
Street vending is a transitional phenomenon that will fade on its own as cities grow richer and formal retail expands, so no policy response is needed.
The passage cites rising vendor numbers against this view.
Cities that regulate vending have consistently reduced congestion and complaints, which shows that regulation works better than tolerance or prohibition.
The passage calls the evidence mixed.
qs.x: This combines the persistence argument with the closing call for well-designed rules. Trap: Choosing an extreme position (ban or celebrate) when the author consistently takes the middle, design-focused position.

qs.q: The author mentions a single piece of fruit and a pair of batteries in order to
o: argue that small purchases are economically unimportant and therefore not worth regulating or counting.
The author uses them to show vending's value.
show that vendors depend on commuters more than on any other customers, since commuters buy in small quantities.
The example illustrates quantity, not customer dependence.
suggest that vendors' goods are of lower quality than those sold in stores, which explains their lower prices.
Quality is never compared.
illustrate demand that formal stores cannot profitably serve given their cost structures.
Correct: The next sentence explains that large stores' costs presuppose bulk sales.
qs.x: The next sentence explains that large stores' costs presuppose bulk sales. Trap: Reading the examples as trivial items rather than as evidence of small-quantity demand.

qs.q: According to the passage, the costs critics attribute to vending would justify prohibition only if
o: formal retailers could not otherwise compete with vendors who avoid rents, licenses, and taxes.
Competition is treated as a fairness issue, not a condition for prohibition.
pedestrian obstruction outweighed the benefits that vending provides to commuters and low-income buyers.
No such weighing is described.
vending could not be regulated and could only be tolerated or eliminated.
Correct: The author states this condition directly in the third paragraph.
vendors refused to pay taxes even when offered a workable way to do so.
The author suggests bringing vendors into the tax system.
qs.x: The author states this condition directly in the third paragraph. Trap: Choosing an option that restates a critic's complaint instead of the condition the author names.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the argument that vending persists because it fills roles formal retail does not?
o: Vendor numbers are highest near transit stations and other places where crowds gather at predictable hours.
This fits the argument about peak demand at particular places.
Many vendors lack formal credentials or documentation that would qualify them for work in the formal retail sector, which is closed to them.
This supports the claim that vending offers entry to the excluded.
Most vendor sales are of the same products, in the same quantities and at the same prices as those at nearby formal stores.
Correct: This implies vendors are not filling a distinct role.
Vendors' overhead is much lower than the rent, utilities, and licensing fees paid by formal stores selling comparable goods.
This supports the flexibility argument.
qs.x: This implies vendors are not filling a distinct role. Trap: Selecting a fact that sounds negative about vendors but actually fits the argument being tested.

qs.q: The author's treatment of the critics' objections can best be described as
o: dismissive, treating the objections as pretexts for excluding the poor from public space entirely.
The author does not question the critics' motives.
resigned, accepting that the costs of vending cannot be reduced by any regulatory design.
The author argues regulation can address them.
alarmed, because the harms to pedestrians and shopkeepers are described as severe and growing.
The tone is analytical rather than alarmed.
even-handed, granting their seriousness while distinguishing among them.
Correct: The author says they deserve to be taken seriously and then sorts them into two kinds.
qs.x: The author says they deserve to be taken seriously and then sorts them into two kinds. Trap: Equating a pro-vendor argument with hostility toward the critics.

qs.q: A city that wished to follow the passage's closing advice would most likely
o: set a fee schedule through city officials alone and enforce it strictly with fines and confiscation of goods from violators.
The author warns against rules written without participation.
convene vendors, shopkeepers, and pedestrian representatives to draft rules for sharing sidewalk space.
Correct: This reflects the idea that rules should be shaped with those they govern and that none of the three is an intruder.
move vendors out of commercial districts to designated peripheral zones where they would not obstruct pedestrians or compete with stores.
This treats vendors as intruders.
stop regulating vending entirely and leave the use of sidewalk space to be settled by individual vendors and shopkeepers.
The author favors well-designed regulation, not none.
qs.x: This reflects the idea that rules should be shaped with those they govern and that none of the three is an intruder. Trap: Mistaking opposition to prohibition for opposition to any regulation.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 3
text: When photography became widely available in the nineteenth century, many commentators greeted it as a machine for preserving the past. A photograph seemed to hold a moment in suspension, immune to the fading and embellishment that corrupt the memories of those who were present. Families commissioned portraits of the dying; governments documented monuments; travelers returned with images of places their neighbors would never see. The camera, it was said, could not lie, and a civilization that possessed it would never again lose its history.

The confidence was misplaced, and the reasons are more interesting than the usual complaint that images can be manipulated. Even an unaltered photograph records a decision. Someone chose the angle, the framing, the moment, and, just as important, what to leave outside the frame. A photograph of a harvest festival may omit the debts that burdened the farmers; a photograph of a factory may show gleaming machinery and no workers. The image is accurate in what it shows and silent about what it excludes, and the silence is easily mistaken for absence. Viewers rarely ask what lay a few feet to the left. A caption adds a further layer of selection, since the words beneath an image tell viewers what to notice and what to ignore.

A subtler difficulty concerns what photographs do to the memories they were meant to protect. Psychologists have long observed that remembering is not retrieval of a stored record but reconstruction, assembled anew each time from fragments and expectations. When a photograph is available, it supplies the fragments. Over years, a person who looks repeatedly at an image of a childhood birthday may come to remember the party as the photograph depicts it, with the remembered scene acquiring the photograph's composition, its vantage point, even its colors. Events that were never photographed, meanwhile, receive no such reinforcement and may fade. The camera, in other words, does not merely preserve the past; it selects the portions of it that will survive in memory, and it does so according to what was photographed rather than what mattered.

This selective effect has consequences that extend beyond the individual. Societies, like persons, remember through the artifacts they have. An archive heavy with images of official ceremonies and light on images of ordinary labor will tend to yield a history of ceremonies. Those who were rarely photographed, because they lacked the means or the standing to commission portraits, are underrepresented in the visual record and thus easier to forget. Photography, which was supposed to democratize memory, has in many periods reproduced the hierarchies of the societies that practiced it.

None of this is an argument for discarding photographs. The remedy for a partial record is a larger and more varied one, together with a habit of reading images as evidence produced by particular people for particular purposes. A photograph read in this way becomes more informative, not less, because its omissions, once noticed, are themselves data. What is required is a shift in how we regard the medium: not as a mirror held up to the past, but as one witness among many in a continuing argument about it.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Early commentators were right that photography democratized historical memory.
The author says it often reproduced hierarchies.
Photography has damaged memory so much that archives should avoid relying on it.
The author says photographs should not be discarded.
Photographs, though once thought to preserve the past faithfully, are selective records that also shape memory and should be read critically alongside other evidence.
Correct: This covers selection, memory, and the closing recommendation.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 4
text: Before the late nineteenth century, most towns kept their own time. Noon was the moment the sun stood highest overhead, and clocks in neighboring towns might differ by several minutes without anyone being troubled. The arrangement worked because few people needed to coordinate with anyone beyond walking distance. The railroad changed this. A train traveling between distant cities crossed many local times in a single journey, and timetables listing arrivals according to a dozen different noons were nearly useless. Railway companies therefore adopted standard time zones, and within a generation most communities had set their clocks to match.

The usual account treats this change as a triumph of practicality, a case of technology demanding rationality and rationality obliging. There is truth in this, but the account leaves out the resistance. Many towns resisted the new time, regarding it as an imposition by distant corporations on local custom. Newspaper editors complained that the railroads had presumed to alter the day itself. Some communities maintained two sets of time, one for the railway station and one for everything else, and a few clung to local time for years. That the resistance eventually faded reveals less about the persuasiveness of the arguments than about the mounting costs of standing apart: a town that kept its own time could not be conveniently reached, and so it gradually lost the commerce that depended on being reachable.

Sociologists have drawn from this episode a broader lesson about how standards spread. A standard is valuable largely because others use it, and its value to any single adopter increases with the number of adopters. Such arrangements tend to be unstable in the early period, when no one wishes to be first, and then abruptly self-reinforcing once a critical mass has been reached. Once most had adopted railway time, holdouts faced pressure not from the railways' power but from the choices of their neighbors, who preferred to deal with those whose clocks agreed with their own.

The adoption of standard time also altered how people experienced the day. When time was local and tied to the sun, it was understood as a feature of the natural world, something observed rather than set. Standard time was visibly conventional: it could be adjusted by agreement, and it applied equally to a place where the sun had risen and one where it had not. As clock time grew detached from the sun, it became easier to treat as a resource to be measured, scheduled, and allocated. Factory managers could compare hours worked; schools could divide the day into uniform periods; workers began to speak of being "on the clock." Whether these developments flowed from standard time or merely coincided with it is difficult to establish, since industrialization was proceeding for independent reasons. But the timing suggests that a shared, conventional time made certain habits of mind easier to acquire.

It would be wrong to conclude that the change was simply imposed on a passive public, or that it was freely chosen. The more accurate description lies between: individuals made rational choices, but the range of choices available to them was determined by decisions others had already made.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 5
text: Listeners who encounter recordings made in the first decades of the twentieth century are often struck by how odd the performances sound. Violinists slide between notes with a persistence that modern players avoid; pianists roll chords and let the hands fall slightly out of synchrony; singers take liberties with tempo that a present-day conductor would not tolerate. The natural reaction is to suppose that these musicians were simply less disciplined than their successors, or that their era had not yet discovered the precision that recording would later demand.

This reaction mistakes a difference in convention for a difference in skill. The performers in question were frequently of extraordinary ability, and their departures from the written score were deliberate. In the tradition they inherited, a score was understood as a sketch rather than a specification; the performer's responsibility was to supply expressive inflection that notation could not capture, and a performance that adhered rigidly to the printed rhythm would have been considered lifeless. The modern ideal, in which the performer's task is to realize the composer's text with minimal intrusion, is itself a historical development, not an eternal standard.

Why did the ideal change? One explanation points to the recording itself. A live performance is heard once, and an idiosyncratic gesture that delights in the moment is forgotten in the next. A recording is heard again and again, and the same gesture, repeated, can begin to grate. Performers who knew their work would be preserved had reason to prefer interpretations that would withstand repetition, and listeners who could compare multiple recordings of the same piece began to notice and prize accuracy. Competition among recordings thus rewarded a kind of precision that concert halls had never demanded.

This explanation is plausible, but it is incomplete. Changes in taste were underway before recording became common, and they were driven partly by composers who grew impatient with what they regarded as performers' liberties. Several prominent composers of the period published increasingly detailed markings and issued public complaints about interpreters who altered their work. The recording industry may have accelerated the shift, but it found a movement already in progress, and it is unlikely to have created it.

There is a further irony. The performers whose styles now seem eccentric left recordings that make it possible to hear what they actually did, and the recordings reveal that written descriptions of their art can be misleading. Critics of the time praised a violinist's "restraint" or a pianist's "fidelity," words that a modern listener, hearing the recordings, would never apply. The vocabulary of praise had meant something different. Without the recordings we would have assumed that earlier musicians played much as we do and that the words meant what they mean to us. The medium that is blamed for standardizing performance has also preserved the evidence that standards were once otherwise.

That evidence invites humility. If conventions that seemed natural to one generation appear strange to the next, we have little reason to believe that our own are exempt from the same fate. Future listeners may find our scrupulous literalism as peculiar as we find the slides and rolled chords of our predecessors.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 6
text: Economists often describe exchange as the trading of goods whose values the parties have compared and found equal enough to make the transaction worthwhile. On this model, a gift is an anomaly: a transfer of value without anything received in return. The standard way of handling the anomaly has been to explain it away, either by treating gifts as disguised self-interest, given to win favor or to be repaid later, or by relegating them to the private sphere of families, where market logic is held not to apply. Anthropologists who have studied societies in which gifts structure much of economic life have argued that both responses miss what gift exchange is for.

In many of these societies, giving creates a relationship rather than settling one. A gift is not equivalent to a payment because it is not meant to close an account. A person who receives a gift acquires an obligation, but the obligation is open-ended: to return something, at some later time, of a kind and amount that cannot be precisely specified. Attempting to repay at once, or with exact equivalence, is understood as an insult, a refusal of the relationship, since it announces that the recipient wishes to owe nothing. The unspecified and deferred quality of the return is not a flaw in the system but its point. Debt that remains outstanding keeps the parties bound to one another.

This analysis helps clarify why gifts and sales feel different even when the objects involved are the same. A commercial transaction is designed to leave the parties independent: after the money changes hands, neither owes the other anything and neither need meet again. A gift is designed to do the opposite. Consider the difference between handing a neighbor cash for a favor and bringing a pie after the neighbor has watched one's house. The cash may be worth more, yet it may seem faintly offensive, because it treats the neighbor as a vendor rather than as someone with whom one expects to remain in a relationship.

It would be a mistake, however, to infer that gift economies are more benevolent than markets. The obligations that bind people can also trap them. A chief who gives lavishly can place rivals under debts they cannot discharge, converting generosity into dominance. In such settings the gift is a weapon as well as a bond, and the person who cannot reciprocate is diminished rather than comforted. The open-ended character of the debt that sustains cooperation also sustains inequality.

Nor are the two systems cleanly separated in modern life. Employers speak of loyalty and offer perquisites that are not strictly wages; merchants cultivate regular customers with small unrequested favors; professionals trade courtesies that no contract requires. Each of these ordinary practices blends the logic of the market with the logic of the gift, and each depends on the ambiguity. When the gift element is made explicit as a calculated inducement, it tends to lose its force, because the recipient recognizes that the relationship being offered is itself being priced.

o: Modern life has replaced gift exchange with market exchange.
The final paragraph says the two remain mixed.
Gift economies are more benevolent than market economies.
The fourth paragraph rejects this inference.
Gift exchange creates and sustains relationships through open-ended obligation, distinguishing it from market exchange, although it can also sustain hierarchy and blends with market practices today.

qs.x: This includes the central claim and the two qualifications. Trap: Selecting the economists' view that the author sets out to criticize.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward the standard economic treatment of gifts is best described as
o: critical, regarding it as explaining the phenomenon away instead of explaining it.
Correct: The author says both standard responses miss what gift exchange is for.
indifferent, offering no evaluation of whether the standard economic treatment is adequate or not.
