passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 7
text: Satire is often defended on the ground that it reforms its targets: by exposing folly to ridicule, the satirist shames people into abandoning it. The defense has a long pedigree among satirists themselves, who have routinely announced reform as their purpose. But the historical record offers little evidence that ridiculed vices diminish under ridicule, and the persistence of the very follies that satirists lampooned centuries ago suggests that something other than correction is at work.

An alternative account locates the function of satire not in its effect on its targets but in its effect on its audience. A satirical piece addresses readers who already share the satirist's judgments and invites them to enjoy the confirmation of those judgments. The pleasure is the pleasure of recognition: the reader laughs because the portrait of the pompous official or the grasping merchant matches an opinion already held. Satire, on this view, does not change minds but consolidates communities, drawing a line between the knowing, who see the joke, and the targets, who do not. A joke that required explanation would fail in just the place where it was meant to succeed.

This account explains several features that the reform theory struggles with. It explains why satire so seldom troubles its targets, who typically are not reading. It explains why the most effective satire is often the most local, depending on allusions that outsiders cannot follow, and why it ages poorly once the allusions are lost. And it explains why satirists in every age have been more popular with those who agree with them than with those they attack, a pattern that would be puzzling if the aim were to persuade the unconverted. Each of these features follows naturally from the community account, whereas the reform account must treat all of them as unfortunate accidents of circumstance.

Yet the community-building theory has its own difficulties. If satire merely confirmed existing opinion, it would be hard to explain why authorities have so frequently feared it, censoring satirists, jailing them, or banning their plays. Rulers are not generally alarmed by entertainments that leave their opponents' views unchanged. The fear suggests that satire does something more than flatter an audience, and one plausible candidate is that it makes dissent publicly speakable. A grievance that individuals harbor privately gains a different status when it is voiced aloud and met with laughter, for the laughter shows each listener that others share the grievance. The effect is not to convert but to coordinate: to turn scattered private opinions into common knowledge.

If this is right, then both traditional and revisionist accounts have captured part of the truth. Satire does not reform its targets, as the defenders claim, but neither is it merely a form of self-congratulation, as the revisionists imply. Its power lies in the space between private opinion and public expression, a space in which a society decides what it is willing to say about itself. That satirists' own stated intentions may be mistaken about this need not surprise us; writers are rarely the best theorists of what their work accomplishes.

Correct: This is the final synthesis of the passage.

qs.x: The author says the fear suggests satire does more than flatter. Trap: Reading the example as support for the account it actually challenges.

o: Satirists report that they intend to reform their targets and that they judge their success by whether reforms follow.

o: Rulers have often censored satirists and burned their works, sometimes imprisoning the authors for years.

Satire depends on local allusions that readers in other places or periods seldom recognize.
This is part of the author's own account.
Documented cases in which many satirized officials changed their conduct after reading the satire.
Correct: This is direct evidence of reform.
Many satirical works are read mainly by people who already share the satirist's views and attitudes.
This is consistent with the passage.
qs.x: This is direct evidence of reform. Trap: Choosing a fact the author already cites as consistent with the argument.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 8
text: When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. The aphorism is cited so often that its force has dulled, but the phenomenon it describes is real and its mechanisms deserve closer attention than the slogan suggests. Consider a school system that wishes to know whether its students are learning to read. It administers a standardized test, and scores on the test are, at first, reasonably good indicators of reading ability: students who read well tend to score well, and the correlation is strong enough to be useful. Then the system attaches consequences to the scores. Schools whose scores rise receive funding; those whose scores fall are sanctioned. The correlation between scores and ability begins to weaken, not because the test has changed but because everyone involved has begun to respond to it.

The responses take several forms. The least troubling is straightforward improvement: teachers examine the test, identify the skills it measures, and teach those skills more effectively. If the test measures reading comprehension and teachers improve comprehension instruction, the system has achieved what it hoped. But the test samples only a portion of what reading involves, and teachers under pressure have reason to concentrate on that portion. Time spent on extended writing, on sustained engagement with long books, or on discussion of ambiguous texts, none of which the test captures, may shrink. Scores may rise while the broader ability they were meant to indicate stagnates. At the far end lie practices that involve no improvement at all, such as the strategic exclusion of weak students from testing or, in documented cases, outright alteration of answer sheets.

It is tempting to treat these responses as moral failures by individuals, but this diagnosis is too convenient. Teachers who narrow the curriculum are responding rationally to the incentives they have been given. If their institution rewards a number, they will produce the number; to expect otherwise is to expect them to sacrifice their schools in the name of a purity that no one has asked of the administrators who designed the system. The failing, if there is one, belongs largely to the design.

Does this mean that measurement should be abandoned? That conclusion would be too hasty. Without measurement, resources are allocated by anecdote and influence, and the students least able to advocate for themselves are the most likely to be overlooked. The more constructive conclusion is that measures are most reliable when they are not the sole basis for consequences, when several different indicators are consulted, and when the indicators are periodically changed so that effort cannot be fixed on a single target. Even these safeguards will not eliminate distortion, but they can reduce the degree to which a measure's usefulness is destroyed by the very attention that makes it matter.

The deeper lesson is that every measure is a proxy, and the gap between proxy and purpose is where gaming takes place. The wider that gap, and the higher the stakes attached to the proxy, the greater the opportunity and the incentive to exploit it.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Teachers who narrow the curriculum in order to raise scores should be disciplined for gaming the tests, since their conduct harms students.
The author calls this diagnosis too convenient.
Attaching high stakes to a measure tends to degrade its value as an indicator, but the remedy is better measurement, not abandonment.
Correct: This covers both the problem and the recommendation.
Test scores never correlate with reading ability, which is why they should not be used to judge schools.
The passage says they correlate at first.
Standardized tests should be abandoned because they cannot capture what reading ability actually involves.
The author calls that conclusion too hasty.
qs.x: This covers both the problem and the recommendation. Trap: Choosing the blame-the-teachers or abandon-the-test reading the author explicitly rejects.

qs.q: According to the passage, the correlation between test scores and reading ability weakens after consequences are attached because
o: students stop reading outside school because test preparation takes up their free time.
This is not mentioned.
schools and teachers begin to respond to the test itself.
Correct: The author says everyone involved begins to respond to it.
the test becomes harder to pass as officials raise the passing standard each year.
The author says the test has not changed.
the test is revised to include new skills that are less closely tied to reading ability.
The author says the test has not changed.
qs.x: The author says everyone involved begins to respond to it. Trap: Missing the explicit statement that the test itself did not change.

qs.q: The author discusses teachers improving comprehension instruction in order to
o: show that responding to a target is not always harmful.
Correct: The author calls this the least troubling response, one that achieves what the system hoped.
argue that the test measures all of what reading involves.
The author says it samples only a portion.
claim that teachers are the main source of distortion.
The author locates the failing largely in design.
show that test tampering is rare.
No rate of tampering is given.
qs.x: The author calls this the least troubling response, one that achieves what the system hoped. Trap: Treating a benign example as evidence for a claim about the test's completeness.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward teachers who narrow the curriculum is best described as
o: approving, regarding narrowing as good teaching because it focuses effort on what is measured.
The author notes the broader ability may stagnate.
understanding, locating the fault chiefly in the system's design.
Correct: The author says they respond rationally to the incentives given.
detached, offering no view of where responsibility for the narrowing of the curriculum lies.
The author clearly assigns responsibility to design.
condemnatory, treating them as morally culpable for harming students to raise their own ratings.
The author calls that diagnosis too convenient.
qs.x: The author says they respond rationally to the incentives given. Trap: Treating an explanation of behavior as approval of it.

qs.q: Which of the following is the best illustration of the 'gap between proxy and purpose' described in the final paragraph?
o: A city stops measuring crime rates altogether after officials conclude that police statistics cannot be trusted.
This abandons measurement, which the author does not recommend.
A company tracks sales using several different indicators so that no single figure can be manipulated.
This is a safeguard, not an exploitation of the gap.
A hospital is judged on surgical survival rates, and surgeons decline to operate on the sickest patients.
Correct: The proxy (survival rate) improves while the purpose (caring for patients) is undermined.
A school improves comprehension instruction after examining the test and then sees both scores and ability rise.
This improves the purpose along with the proxy.
qs.x: The proxy (survival rate) improves while the purpose (caring for patients) is undermined. Trap: Choosing an example about measurement in general rather than one in which the proxy is exploited.

qs.q: Which finding would most weaken the author's suggestion that consulting several indicators and rotating them reduces distortion?
o: Schools quickly learn to raise every indicator in the rotation through the same narrow teaching practices.
Correct: This shows the safeguards do not reduce gaming.
Schools rarely exclude weak students from testing when several indicators are used, even when their ratings are at stake.
This supports the suggestion.
Test scores are somewhat correlated with other indicators of reading ability, such as grades and teacher evaluations.
Correlation does not show that safeguards fail.
Indicators that are never changed are gamed more heavily over time than rotated ones.
This supports the suggestion.
qs.x: This shows the safeguards do not reduce gaming. Trap: Selecting a finding that sounds critical of testing but actually supports the author's recommendation.

passages.title: FL01 · CARS · Passage 9
text: In the late twentieth century, the cleaning of several celebrated paintings provoked a controversy that revealed how little agreement exists about what a restorer is trying to restore. Conservators removed layers of aged varnish and grime, and the canvases emerged startlingly bright, their blues and reds more vivid than viewers had known. Admirers rejoiced that the artists' true colors had been recovered. Critics protested that the cleaning had stripped away subtle glazes, flattened the shadows, and produced a clarity the artists never intended.

Both sides assumed there was a determinate answer to the question of how the painting "really" looked. The admirers equated the original with the state of the painting at the moment it was finished; the critics equated it with the painting as it had come to be known and, in some cases, as the artist might have anticipated it would mature. Neither assumption is silly. Painters of earlier centuries knew that their pigments would darken and that varnish would yellow, and some applied final glazes expecting the surface to settle into a particular harmony. To remove everything added by time may therefore be to remove part of the work as its maker conceived it. At the same time, to leave a painting dimmed beneath layers that obscure its drawing and color is to deny viewers access to what the maker actually put on the canvas.

The dispute is complicated by the fact that the physical evidence is ambiguous. A conservator can distinguish original paint from later varnish under magnification and chemical analysis, but cannot always determine whether a thin, translucent layer was part of the artist's design or a later addition. In such cases the decision rests on judgment about the artist's intentions, and those intentions must be inferred from the work itself, from fragments of documentary evidence, and from comparison with other paintings, each a source of uncertainty. A restorer who claims to be merely uncovering the truth is concealing the interpretive character of the act.

This suggests that the controversy is less about technique than about what we value in old pictures. Those who prize authenticity of materials will favor minimal intervention, preferring a painting that shows its age honestly to one that has been made to look new. Those who prize the visual experience the artist designed will favor more aggressive cleaning, accepting some risk of loss for the sake of legibility. These priorities are not reducible to facts about the paint; they are commitments, and reasonable people can hold either. A restorer's decision about how far to clean is therefore a decision about which of these goods to sacrifice, and no measurement of the paint can make that decision on the restorer's behalf.

The best practice, accordingly, is probably neither bold nor timid but transparent. Restorers should document each stage of treatment, retain samples of removed material when possible, and avoid permanent measures that foreclose later reconsideration. Because the judgments embodied in any restoration will in time look as dated as the varnish they replaced, the most valuable thing a conservator can leave is the means by which a future generation can undo them.

qs.q: Which of the following best states the main idea of the passage?
o: Aggressive cleaning is justified because it recovers the artist's true colors, which later varnish and grime have hidden for centuries.
The author calls this one of two assumptions that are not determinate.
Restoration disputes arise because restoring involves interpretive judgments and competing values, so transparent, reversible treatment is best.
Correct: This covers the cause of the dispute and the recommendation.
The critics of the cleaning were correct and the admirers mistaken, since the cleaned surface lacks the harmony the artist intended.
The author says neither assumption is silly.
Minimal intervention is always the best policy for old paintings, since any removal of material permanently destroys evidence of the artist's intentions and the work's history.
The author says both priorities are legitimate commitments.
qs.x: This covers the cause of the dispute and the recommendation. Trap: Siding with one party in the controversy when the author declines to.

qs.q: The author claims physical evidence cannot settle restoration disputes because
o: documentary evidence about artists' intentions is almost always absent from the historical record altogether.
The author says it exists in fragments.
chemical analysis cannot distinguish paint from varnish at all, even with modern instruments and samples.
The author says conservators can usually distinguish them.
painters of earlier centuries disagreed about varnish, so no single practice can be assumed.
No such disagreement is mentioned.
conservators cannot always tell whether a thin translucent layer was part of the artist's design.
Correct: The author says this directly in the third paragraph.
qs.x: The author says this directly in the third paragraph. Trap: Overstating the ambiguity into an inability to distinguish any layers.

qs.q: The statement that painters knew pigments would darken and varnish would yellow serves to
o: suggest that earlier painters were careless about durability.
They are described as aware and planning for aging.
prove that artists wanted their paintings to appear dark.
The passage says only that some expected a harmony to settle.
argue that restorers have misled the public.
The author does not say this.
show that the critics' position has a reasonable basis.
Correct: It supports the idea that aged surfaces can be part of the work as conceived.
qs.x: It supports the idea that aged surfaces can be part of the work as conceived. Trap: Over-reading a supporting detail as proof of a stronger claim.

qs.q: The author's attitude toward a restorer who claims merely to be uncovering the truth is best described as
o: skeptical, because the claim hides the interpretive nature of the work.
Correct: The author says it conceals the interpretive character of the act.
hostile, accusing the restorer of fraud and of deliberately misleading museum visitors.
The author describes concealment of interpretation, not fraud.
admiring of the restorer's confidence in being able to recover the original surface.
The author criticizes the claim.
indifferent to what restorers claim, since claims have no bearing on how paintings are treated.
The author takes a clear position.
qs.x: The author says it conceals the interpretive character of the act. Trap: Escalating a methodological criticism into an accusation of dishonesty.

qs.q: A museum is choosing between two plans for a darkened painting. Plan X removes all later layers permanently. Plan Y removes only clearly later grime, documents each step, keeps samples, and uses reversible methods. The author would most likely favor
o: neither plan, because any intervention falsifies the work and any restoration fabricates it.
The author does not oppose all intervention.
Plan X, because it uncovers the painting as the artist finished it and removes every later addition.
The author says this is an assumption, not a settled fact.
Plan Y, because it guarantees that the original appearance will be recovered and later critics will agree.
The author says no treatment guarantees that.
Plan Y, because it preserves the means for future generations to reconsider today's judgments.
Correct: The author recommends documentation and avoiding permanent measures.
qs.x: The author recommends documentation and avoiding permanent measures. Trap: Choosing the right plan for the wrong reason, such as a guarantee of authenticity the author denies exists.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 1
text: A student studies a 0.50 kg wooden block sliding from rest down a 2.0 m long plank whose angle θ with the horizontal can be adjusted. For each angle, the student releases the block, uses photogates to measure the time needed to travel the full 2.0 m, and averages five trials. The plank surface is uniform, and separate measurements gave a coefficient of static friction of 0.25 and a coefficient of kinetic friction of 0.20 between block and plank. Use g = 9.8 m/s² and neglect air resistance. At 10° the block did not move when released, even after a gentle tap. The student reasons that the acceleration down the plank depends on both the component of gravity along the plank and the friction force opposing the motion, and she compares predictions from a free-body diagram analysis with her data. The predicted times agreed with the measured times to within 2%. Results for the other angles are shown in Table 1 and Figure 1.

qs.q: What is the acceleration of the block down the plank at an angle of 30°?
o: 3.2 m/s²
Correct: a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ) = 9.8(0.500 − 0.20 × 0.866) = 3.2 m/s².
4.9 m/s²
4.9 m/s² is g sin 30° and ignores friction.
8.5 m/s²
8.5 m/s² is g cos 30°, which is the component of gravity perpendicular to the plank.
1.7 m/s²
1.7 m/s² is only the deceleration due to friction (μk g cos 30°), not the net acceleration.
qs.x: a = g(sinθ − μk cosθ) = 9.8(0.500 − 0.20 × 0.866) = 3.2 m/s². Trap: Using g sinθ alone and forgetting that kinetic friction subtracts from the net force along the plank.

qs.q: Which statement best explains why the block did not slide at 10°?
o: Kinetic friction exceeded the component of gravity along the plank.
Kinetic friction only acts once the block is sliding, and it is smaller than the maximum static friction.
The normal force from the plank was zero at that angle.
The normal force is mg cosθ, which is nonzero at every angle below 90°.
The component of gravity along the plank was smaller than the maximum static friction force.
Correct: At 10°, mg sinθ is about 0.85 N while the maximum static friction is μs mg cosθ, about 1.2 N, so static friction can fully cancel the gravitational pull along the plank (tan 10° < 0.25).
The weight of the block was balanced by the normal force, so no net force acted on it.
The normal force balances only the perpendicular component of weight, not the full weight; the issue is the balance along the plank.
qs.x: At 10°, mg sinθ is about 0.85 N while the maximum static friction is μs mg cosθ, about 1.2 N, so static friction can fully cancel the gravitational pull along the plank (tan 10° < 0.25). Trap: Saying the weight is balanced by the normal force, which ignores that the normal force balances only the perpendicular component.

qs.q: What is the magnitude of the kinetic friction force on the block while it slides at 30°?
o: Correct: f = μk N = μk m g cosθ = 0.20 × 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 0.85 N.
0.98 N is μk m g, which uses the full weight instead of the normal force on an incline.
2.5 N is mg sin 30°, the driving component of gravity, not friction.
0.49 N results from using sin 30° instead of cos 30° for the normal force.
qs.x: f = μk N = μk m g cosθ = 0.20 × 0.50 × 9.8 × 0.866 = 0.85 N. Trap: Using the full weight mg as the normal force on a tilted surface instead of mg cosθ.

qs.q: What is the speed of the block at the bottom of the plank when θ = 40°?
o: 3.1 m/s is 4.4/√2 and has no basis in the data; it would result from mishandling the square root in v = √(2ad).
6.3 m/s is √(2gd), the speed that would result from dropping through 2.0 m with no plank, ignoring both the angle and friction.
Correct: The mean time is 0.91 s over 2.0 m from rest, so a = 2d/t² = 4.8 m/s², and v = at = 4.8 × 0.91 = 4.4 m/s (equivalently v = 2d/t).
8.8 m/s is double the correct final speed, which would result from applying the factor of 2 in v = 2d/t twice.
qs.x: The mean time is 0.91 s over 2.0 m from rest, so a = 2d/t² = 4.8 m/s², and v = at = 4.8 × 0.91 = 4.4 m/s (equivalently v = 2d/t). Trap: Treating the average speed (d/t = 2.2 m/s) as the final speed.

qs.q: What is the work done by kinetic friction on the block over the full 2.0 m at 30°?
o: +1.7 J has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign; friction points opposite to the motion.
−4.9 J reuses the value of mg sin 30° (4.9 N) as if it were an energy; the distance of 2.0 m is not applied, and friction, not gravity, is asked about.
−0.85 J omits multiplying by the 2.0 m distance, so it is only the force value.
Correct: W = −f d = −(0.85 N)(2.0 m) = −1.7 J; friction opposes the displacement, so the work is negative.
qs.x: W = −f d = −(0.85 N)(2.0 m) = −1.7 J; friction opposes the displacement, so the work is negative. Trap: Reporting the friction force in newtons as the work, or giving work done by friction a positive sign.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 2
text: Atherosclerotic plaque narrows arteries, and a physician models the effect with a horizontal rigid tube whose radius changes along its length. Blood is treated as an ideal, incompressible fluid of density 1060 kg/m³ with no viscosity. In the normal segment the radius is 4.0 mm and the blood speed is 0.30 m/s. Narrowed segments of smaller radius are considered one at a time. Using the continuity equation and Bernoulli's equation, the speed in each narrowed segment and the drop in pressure relative to the normal segment were calculated and are given in Table 1. Figure 1 plots speed against radius. In a real artery, viscosity cannot be ignored. For steady laminar flow of a viscous fluid in a long, narrow tube, Poiseuille's law states that the volumetric flow rate is proportional to the pressure difference across the tube and to the fourth power of the tube radius, and inversely proportional to the tube length and the fluid viscosity.

qs.q: What is the volumetric flow rate of blood through the normal segment?
o: 3.8 mL/s
3.8 mL/s is one quarter of the correct value and would come from dividing by 4.
60 mL/s
60 mL/s is four times the correct value, as if the radius were doubled.
15 mL/s
Correct: Q = Av = π(4.0 × 10⁻³ m)²(0.30 m/s) = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s, which is 15 cm³/s = 15 mL/s.
1.5 mL/s
1.5 mL/s is off by a factor of 10 from a unit conversion error (1 m³ = 10⁶ mL).
qs.x: Q = Av = π(4.0 × 10⁻³ m)²(0.30 m/s) = 1.5 × 10⁻⁵ m³/s, which is 15 cm³/s = 15 mL/s. Trap: Converting m³/s to mL/s incorrectly, or using the diameter or radius without squaring it.

qs.q: Exercise increases the total flow rate through the model by 50% while the geometry is unchanged. What is the speed in the 2.0 mm radius segment?
o: 2.7 m/s results from multiplying by 1.5 twice, as if speed scaled with the square of flow rate.
Correct: For a fixed cross-sectional area, speed is proportional to flow rate, so v = 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.8 m/s.
1.5 m/s adds 0.30 m/s to the tabulated speed rather than scaling it.
0.8 m/s divides by 1.5 instead of multiplying, which would imply flow rate decreased.
qs.x: For a fixed cross-sectional area, speed is proportional to flow rate, so v = 1.20 × 1.5 = 1.8 m/s. Trap: Applying the 50% increase as an additive change or squaring it instead of scaling speed proportionally.

qs.q: According to Table 1, the pressure drop in the 2.0 mm segment is 716 Pa. Approximately what is this in mmHg? (1 mmHg = 133 Pa)
o: 54 mmHg
54 mmHg is a factor of 10 too large.
5.4 mmHg
Correct: 716 Pa ÷ 133 Pa/mmHg = 5.4 mmHg. Pressure falls in the narrow segment because its higher speed means higher kinetic energy per volume (Bernoulli).
0.54 mmHg
0.54 mmHg is a factor of 10 too small.
716 mmHg
716 mmHg reports the value in pascals with the wrong unit and no conversion.
qs.x: 716 Pa ÷ 133 Pa/mmHg = 5.4 mmHg. Pressure falls in the narrow segment because its higher speed means higher kinetic energy per volume (Bernoulli). Trap: Misplacing the decimal in a unit conversion, or forgetting to convert Pa to mmHg.

qs.q: In a real viscous artery of fixed length and fixed pressure difference, what happens to the volumetric flow rate if the radius is cut in half?
o: It decreases by a factor of 16.
Correct: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r reduces Q by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16.
It decreases by a factor of 4.
A factor of 4 is the result of the ideal-fluid continuity relation (speed ∝ 1/r²) and neglects the r⁴ dependence of viscous flow.
It decreases by a factor of 2.
A factor of 2 would imply flow rate is directly proportional to radius.
It increases by a factor of 4.
Flow does not increase; in the narrower tube resistance rises sharply, so flow falls.
qs.x: Poiseuille's law gives Q ∝ r⁴, so halving r reduces Q by (1/2)⁴ = 1/16. Trap: Using the continuity-equation relation for speed (1/r²) instead of the r⁴ dependence of viscous flow rate.

h: Pressure drop relative to normal segment (Pa)

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 3
text: A concentration cell is built from two copper electrodes, each immersed in its own beaker of aqueous CuSO₄, with the beakers joined by a salt bridge. The Cu²⁺ concentration in one beaker is fixed at 1.0 M, and the concentration in the other beaker is varied. At 25 °C the cell potential is given by E = (0.0592/n) log([Cu²⁺] in the concentrated half-cell ÷ [Cu²⁺] in the dilute half-cell), where n = 2 for this reaction. For each dilute concentration, the open-circuit potential was measured with a voltmeter of very high resistance. The cell was then connected across a 100 Ω resistor, and the potential difference across the resistor was measured. The results appear in Table 1, and Figure 1 plots the open-circuit potential against −log[Cu²⁺] of the dilute half-cell. The difference between the open-circuit potential and the potential across the resistor is due to the internal resistance of the cell, which behaves like a resistor in series with an ideal source.

qs.q: Which description of the electrode reactions and electron flow is correct when the cell operates?
o: Cu(s) is oxidized in the 1.0 M half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Oxidizing in the concentrated cell would make concentrations more unequal, which is not spontaneous.
Cu(s) is oxidized in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the 1.0 M half-cell.

Correct: The spontaneous process evens out the concentrations: Cu oxidizes in the dilute cell (anode), raising its [Cu²⁺], and electrons travel to the 1.0 M cell where Cu²⁺ is reduced (cathode), lowering that [Cu²⁺].
Cu²⁺ is reduced in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Reduction takes place at the cathode, which is the 1.0 M half-cell, and electrons always flow toward the cathode.
Cu(s) is oxidized in the dilute half-cell, and electrons flow through the wire toward the dilute half-cell.
Electrons flow from anode to cathode, so they cannot flow toward the anode.
qs.x: The spontaneous process evens out the concentrations: Cu oxidizes in the dilute cell (anode), raising its [Cu²⁺], and electrons travel to the 1.0 M cell where Cu²⁺ is reduced (cathode), lowering that [Cu²⁺]. Trap: Forgetting that electrons flow from the anode to the cathode through the external wire.

qs.q: What open-circuit potential is expected when the dilute half-cell is 1.0 × 10⁻⁴ M Cu²⁺?
o: 0.059 V corresponds to a dilute concentration of 0.010 M (log = 2).
Correct: E = 0.0296 × log(1.0/1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.0296 × 4 = 0.118 V, consistent with the linear trend in Figure 1.
0.237 V comes from using 0.0592 instead of 0.0296 (forgetting to divide by n = 2).
0.030 V corresponds to a dilute concentration of 0.10 M (log = 1).
qs.x: E = 0.0296 × log(1.0/1.0 × 10⁻⁴) = 0.0296 × 4 = 0.118 V, consistent with the linear trend in Figure 1. Trap: Using 0.0592 without dividing by n = 2 electrons.

qs.q: When the dilute half-cell is 0.010 M, what is the current through the 100 Ω resistor?
o: Correct: I = V/R = 0.0548 V ÷ 100 Ω = 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ A = 0.55 mA, using the potential actually measured across the resistor.
0.59 mA uses the open-circuit potential (0.0592 V), which is not the voltage across the resistor under load.
5.5 A is a factor of 10⁴ too large, a conversion error.
0.055 mA is a factor of 10 too small.
qs.x: I = V/R = 0.0548 V ÷ 100 Ω = 5.5 × 10⁻⁴ A = 0.55 mA, using the potential actually measured across the resistor. Trap: Using the open-circuit EMF rather than the terminal potential across the resistor in Ohm's law.

qs.q: Based on the 0.010 M row of Table 1, what is the internal resistance of the cell?
o: Correct: The internal drop is 0.0592 − 0.0548 = 0.0044 V at I = 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ A, so r = 0.0044/5.48 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 Ω.
80 Ω is a factor of 10 too large.
0.80 Ω is a factor of 10 too small.
108 Ω is the total series resistance (load plus internal), not the internal resistance alone.
qs.x: The internal drop is 0.0592 − 0.0548 = 0.0044 V at I = 5.48 × 10⁻⁴ A, so r = 0.0044/5.48 × 10⁻⁴ = 8.0 Ω. Trap: Reporting the total circuit resistance rather than subtracting the 100 Ω load.

qs.q: If the cell is left connected across the resistor for a long time, what happens to the open-circuit potential?
o: It increases because Cu²⁺ accumulates in the dilute half-cell.
Accumulating Cu²⁺ in the dilute side reduces the concentration ratio, so E falls rather than rises.
It decreases toward zero as the two Cu²⁺ concentrations approach each other.
Correct: Discharge raises [Cu²⁺] in the dilute cell and lowers it in the concentrated cell, so the log term in the Nernst equation falls toward zero, and E reaches 0 V at equilibrium (Q = 1, ΔG = 0).
It remains constant because the copper electrodes are not consumed overall.
Although copper metal is conserved, the potential depends on the concentration ratio, which changes.
It decreases toward zero because the copper electrodes become identical in mass.
The potential depends on ion concentrations, not on electrode masses.
qs.x: Discharge raises [Cu²⁺] in the dilute cell and lowers it in the concentrated cell, so the log term in the Nernst equation falls toward zero, and E reaches 0 V at equilibrium (Q = 1, ΔG = 0). Trap: Assuming E is fixed because the electrode material is unchanged, when it depends on concentration ratio.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 4
text: Doppler ultrasound estimates blood speed by measuring the frequency shift of echoes from moving red blood cells. A probe emits sound of frequency f₀ = 5.0 MHz into soft tissue, in which sound travels at c = 1540 m/s. For blood moving at speed v much less than c, with the beam making an angle θ with the flow direction, the magnitude of the frequency shift is Δf = 2f₀v cosθ / c. A technician tests a phantom in which fluid flows at a constant 0.50 m/s, varying the angle between the probe and the flow. The measured shifts agree with the equation and are shown in Table 1. In a separate measurement through deep tissue, the echo returning from a boundary had an intensity equal to one-thousandth of the intensity of the transmitted pulse. The technician reports attenuation in decibels, where the change in sound level is β = 10 log(I₂/I₁). Assume sound is a longitudinal wave in all media discussed.

qs.q: At θ = 0°, what frequency shift would be measured for blood flowing at 0.80 m/s?
o: 2600 Hz is half the correct value and would come from wrongly applying cos 60° or halving.
3250 Hz is the value for 0.50 m/s and does not account for the faster flow.
8300 Hz multiplies by 1.6 twice, treating Δf as proportional to v².
Correct: Δf is proportional to v. At 0°, 3247 Hz × (0.80/0.50) = 5195 Hz, about 5200 Hz.
qs.x: Δf is proportional to v. At 0°, 3247 Hz × (0.80/0.50) = 5195 Hz, about 5200 Hz. Trap: Squaring the speed ratio even though the shift is linear in v.

qs.q: Why does the equation for Δf contain a factor of 2?
o: The ultrasound travels to the blood and back, doubling the wavelength.
The round trip does not change the wavelength by a factor of 2; the shift arises from motion.
Blood cells move in both directions along the vessel, so two shifts add together.
Blood flows in only one direction, and opposite directions would give shifts of opposite sign, not additive.
Sound waves in tissue have both longitudinal and transverse components, each shifted once.
Sound in fluids is purely longitudinal, as the passage states.
The blood cells first act as moving receivers of the transmitted wave and then as moving sources of the reflected wave, so the shift occurs twice.
Correct: A moving observer hears a shifted frequency, and the cell then re-emits that shifted frequency as a moving source, giving a second shift of nearly the same size.
qs.x: A moving observer hears a shifted frequency, and the cell then re-emits that shifted frequency as a moving source, giving a second shift of nearly the same size. Trap: Attributing the factor of 2 to the round-trip distance rather than to the double Doppler effect.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the 5.0 MHz ultrasound in soft tissue?
o: 3.1 mm
3.1 mm is a factor of 10 too large.
0.031 mm is a factor of 10 too small.
7.7 mm
7.7 mm comes from dividing f by c in the wrong units or confusing MHz with kHz (1540/2.0 × 10⁵).
qs.x: λ = c/f = 1540 m/s ÷ 5.0 × 10⁶ Hz = 3.1 × 10⁻⁴ m = 0.31 mm. Trap: Mishandling powers of 10 when converting MHz to Hz or meters to millimeters.

qs.q: What is the attenuation, in decibels, of the echo described in the passage relative to the transmitted pulse?
o: 20 dB
20 dB would correspond to a hundred fold decrease in intensity.
3 dB
3 dB would correspond to roughly a factor of 2 and results from forgetting the factor of 10 times the logarithm exponent.
30 dB
Correct: β = 10 log(10⁻³) = −30 dB, so the echo is 30 dB below the transmitted pulse.
300 dB
300 dB is a factor of 10 too large, arising from multiplying the exponent by 100.
qs.x: β = 10 log(10⁻³) = −30 dB, so the echo is 30 dB below the transmitted pulse. Trap: Taking the logarithm exponent (3) as the decibel value, which forgets to multiply by 10.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 5
text: Technetium-99m (Tc-99m) is a metastable nuclear isomer widely used for diagnostic imaging. It is obtained from a generator in which molybdenum-99 (atomic number 42) undergoes β⁻ decay, producing Tc-99m. Tc-99m then decays to the ground state of technetium-99 by emitting a γ photon of energy 140 keV. A technician isolates a sample of pure Tc-99m and measures its activity in a dose calibrator every 6.0 hours for one day. The data in Table 1 show that the activity is halved during each 6.0 hour interval. Figure 1 plots the natural logarithm of the activity against time. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. A decay constant λ and the half-life t½ are related by t½ = ln 2/λ, where ln 2 = 0.693. Radioactive decay is a first-order process, so the activity A at time t obeys A = A₀e^(−λt), and a plot of ln A against t is a straight line with slope −λ. Because the γ photon carries no charge and no mass, the emission leaves the nucleus with the same numbers of protons and neutrons that it had before the transition. Clinically, the short half-life limits the radiation dose to the patient.

qs.q: What is the decay constant of Tc-99m?
o: 0.17 h⁻¹ is 1/6.0 and omits the factor of ln 2.
Correct: λ = ln 2 / t½ = 0.693 / 6.0 h = 0.12 h⁻¹, which is also the magnitude of the slope in Figure 1 (−0.116 h⁻¹).
8.7 h⁻¹ is t½/ln 2, an inverted relationship.
4.2 h⁻¹ is 6.0 × 0.693, which multiplies rather than divides.
qs.x: λ = ln 2 / t½ = 0.693 / 6.0 h = 0.12 h⁻¹, which is also the magnitude of the slope in Figure 1 (−0.116 h⁻¹). Trap: Using 1/t½ as the decay constant and forgetting the ln 2 factor.

qs.q: If the sample were measured again 30 hours after the first measurement, what activity would be expected?
o: 6.3 MBq
6.3 MBq corresponds to six half-lives (36 h).
25 MBq
25 MBq is the measured value at 24 h (four half-lives).
12.5 MBq
Correct: 30 h is five half-lives, so A = 400 MBq / 2⁵ = 12.5 MBq.
50 MBq
50 MBq is the measured value at 18 h (three half-lives).
qs.x: 30 h is five half-lives, so A = 400 MBq / 2⁵ = 12.5 MBq. Trap: Miscounting half-lives (30 h/6 h = 5) or reading the nearest table value.

qs.q: Which statement correctly describes the decay of Tc-99m to Tc-99?
o: The nucleus emits a β⁻ particle, increasing the atomic number by 1.
β⁻ decay is how Mo-99 becomes Tc-99m, not how Tc-99m becomes Tc-99; the product here is still technetium.
The nucleus emits a γ photon and moves to a lower energy state, with its mass number and atomic number unchanged.
Correct: An isomeric transition releases excess nuclear energy as a γ photon only, so protons and neutrons are the same before and after (99m to 99).
The nucleus emits an α particle, decreasing the mass number by 4.
An α decay would produce a different element with A = 95.
The nucleus captures an inner electron, decreasing the atomic number by 1.
Electron capture would give molybdenum (Z = 42), but the product is technetium-99.
qs.x: An isomeric transition releases excess nuclear energy as a γ photon only, so protons and neutrons are the same before and after (99m to 99). Trap: Confusing the β decay that forms Tc-99m with the γ emission by which Tc-99m decays.

qs.q: What is the wavelength of the 140 keV γ photon?
o: 8.9 nm
8.9 nm is a factor of 1000 too large, from mixing up nm and pm.
0.89 pm is a factor of 10 too small.
89 pm
89 pm is a factor of 10 too large.
8.9 pm
Correct: λ = hc/E = 1240 eV·nm ÷ 1.40 × 10⁵ eV = 8.9 × 10⁻³ nm = 8.9 pm.
qs.x: λ = hc/E = 1240 eV·nm ÷ 1.40 × 10⁵ eV = 8.9 × 10⁻³ nm = 8.9 pm. Trap: Losing track of the factor of 1000 between nanometers and picometers.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 6
text: Colligative properties depend on the number of dissolved particles rather than their identity. A student measures the freezing-point depression, ΔTf, of aqueous solutions that are each 0.50 molal. The van't Hoff factor i is defined as the measured ΔTf divided by the ΔTf expected if the solute did not dissociate (Kf = 1.86 °C·kg/mol for water). The ideal values of i are 1 for glucose, 2 for NaCl, 3 for CaCl₂, and 2 for MgSO₄. Results are given in Table 1. For comparison, the boiling-point elevation constant of water is Kb = 0.512 °C·kg/mol. For osmotic pressure, Π = iMRT, with R = 0.0821 L·atm/(mol·K). Assume that for these dilute solutions the molarity is approximately equal to the molality, and that measured i values at 0.50 m apply at 25 °C. The student also notes that all measurements used the same pure solvent, that the solutes are non-volatile, and that the measured values differ from the ideal ones for some salts because interactions between ions in solution reduce their effective independence. Molar masses should be taken from a periodic table when needed.

qs.q: What freezing-point depression is expected for a 0.20 m aqueous glucose solution?
o: 0.93 °C is the value at 0.50 m and ignores the lower concentration.
0.74 °C would result from multiplying by 2 as if glucose dissociated into two ions.
Correct: Glucose does not dissociate, so ΔTf = i Kf m = 1 × 1.86 × 0.20 = 0.37 °C.
0.19 °C is roughly Kf × m divided by 2, an arbitrary halving.
qs.x: Glucose does not dissociate, so ΔTf = i Kf m = 1 × 1.86 × 0.20 = 0.37 °C. Trap: Applying a van't Hoff factor greater than 1 to a nonelectrolyte.

qs.q: Which explanation best accounts for the van't Hoff factor of MgSO₄ being much lower than 2?
o: MgSO₄ is a molecular compound that does not dissociate in water.
MgSO₄ is an ionic salt that dissolves to give ions; incomplete dissociation does not mean no dissociation (i = 1.18 > 1).
Mg²⁺ ions react with water to form Mg(s) and H₂.
Magnesium ions are not reduced by water under these conditions.
The sulfate ion is much larger than chloride, so it lowers the freezing point of water less per ion.
Colligative properties depend on particle number, not ion size.
The highly charged Mg²⁺ and SO₄²⁻ ions associate into ion pairs, reducing the effective number of independent particles.
Correct: Divalent ions have high charge density and attract each other strongly, so some stay paired even in solution; the measured i is therefore only 1.18.
qs.x: Divalent ions have high charge density and attract each other strongly, so some stay paired even in solution; the measured i is therefore only 1.18. Trap: Assuming colligative effects depend on the size or identity of ions rather than on particle count.

qs.q: Approximately what osmotic pressure would a 0.50 M NaCl solution have at 25 °C, using the measured i from Table 1?
o: 12 atm
12 atm is the value with i = 1 and ignores dissociation.
36 atm
36 atm would arise from using i = 3, the value for CaCl₂.
48 atm
48 atm comes from doubling the correct answer, for example by using i = 2 and then doubling again.
24 atm
Correct: Π = iMRT = 1.94 × 0.50 × 0.0821 × 298 = 23.7 atm, or about 24 atm.
qs.x: Π = iMRT = 1.94 × 0.50 × 0.0821 × 298 = 23.7 atm, or about 24 atm. Trap: Omitting the van't Hoff factor, or using the wrong number of ions.

qs.q: What is the boiling point of the 0.50 m glucose solution at 1 atm?
o: 99.74 °C subtracts the elevation, but dissolved solute raises the boiling point.
100.93 °C uses Kf (and the freezing-point value 0.93) rather than Kb.
100.51 °C results from doubling ΔTb, treating glucose as dissociating into two particles.
Correct: ΔTb = i Kb m = 1 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.26 °C, which raises the boiling point from 100.00 °C to 100.26 °C.
qs.x: ΔTb = i Kb m = 1 × 0.512 × 0.50 = 0.26 °C, which raises the boiling point from 100.00 °C to 100.26 °C. Trap: Using the freezing-point constant for a boiling-point calculation.

qs.q: What mass of CaCl₂ (molar mass 111 g/mol) should be dissolved in 500 g of water to prepare a 0.50 m solution?
o: 55.5 g is for 1.0 kg of water (0.50 mol).
13.9 g is 0.125 mol, half the required amount, as if only 250 g of water were used.
Correct: Moles needed = 0.50 mol/kg × 0.500 kg = 0.25 mol, and 0.25 mol × 111 g/mol = 27.7 g.
111 g is a full mole, which would give 2.0 m in 500 g of water.
qs.x: Moles needed = 0.50 mol/kg × 0.500 kg = 0.25 mol, and 0.25 mol × 111 g/mol = 27.7 g. Trap: Using the full kilogram of solvent when only 500 g is used.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 7
text: A student compares boiling points to evaluate the role of intermolecular forces. Table 1 lists four compounds of nearly equal molar mass but different functional groups, along with their normal boiling points. Figure 1 shows the normal boiling points of the straight-chain alkanes from methane (C₁) to hexane (C₆). Pentane and diethyl ether are both volatile liquids that cannot donate hydrogen bonds to themselves. Butanone has a carbonyl group but no O–H bond. 1-Butanol has an O–H group. The student notes that a boiling point reflects the energy needed to overcome intermolecular attractions in the liquid, such as London dispersion forces, dipole–dipole interactions, and hydrogen bonding. London dispersion forces generally increase with the number of electrons and with the surface area available for contact between molecules. The student hypothesizes that the functional group matters more than molar mass when molar masses are similar. The boiling points in the table were measured at 1 atm. The student expects that, among compounds of similar size and shape, the strongest net intermolecular attractions will produce the highest boiling point, and she will test this idea against both datasets.

qs.q: Which intermolecular force best explains why 1-butanol has the highest boiling point in Table 1?
o: Stronger London dispersion forces because 1-butanol has a larger molar mass than pentane
The molar mass differs by only 2 g/mol from pentane (72 vs 74), so dispersion forces cannot account for a 81 °C difference.
Hydrogen bonding between O–H groups of neighboring molecules, in addition to dispersion forces
Correct: 1-Butanol has an O–H group that is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving much stronger attractions than the other compounds of similar mass.
Covalent bonding between neighboring 1-butanol molecules
Liquid butanol consists of discrete molecules; the intermolecular attractions are non-covalent.
Ion–dipole interactions between 1-butanol molecules
No ions are present in pure 1-butanol.
qs.x: 1-Butanol has an O–H group that is both a hydrogen-bond donor and acceptor, giving much stronger attractions than the other compounds of similar mass. Trap: Attributing a large boiling point difference to molar mass when masses are nearly identical.

qs.q: Diethyl ether has a polar C–O–C bond, yet its boiling point is almost the same as that of pentane. What is the best explanation?
o: Diethyl ether is nonpolar, so its only intermolecular force is dispersion, unlike pentane.
Diethyl ether is polar; it is the extent of that polarity that is small.
Pentane forms hydrogen bonds that offset its lack of a dipole.
Pentane has no electronegative atoms and cannot hydrogen bond.
Diethyl ether has only a weak net dipole and cannot hydrogen bond to itself, so dispersion forces dominate in both liquids.
Correct: The bent C–O–C geometry produces a modest dipole, but without an O–H group there is no hydrogen bonding, and the dispersion forces of two similar-sized molecules are comparable.
Diethyl ether forms hydrogen bonds with itself, but these are canceled by its larger molar mass.
Diethyl ether has no hydrogen on oxygen, so it cannot donate hydrogen bonds to itself.
qs.x: The bent C–O–C geometry produces a modest dipole, but without an O–H group there is no hydrogen bonding, and the dispersion forces of two similar-sized molecules are comparable. Trap: Assuming any molecule with oxygen can hydrogen bond with itself.

qs.q: Based on the trend in Figure 1, which value is the most reasonable estimate of the boiling point of heptane (C₇)?
o: About 70 °C
About 70 °C would imply that adding a carbon has almost no effect, contradicting the clear upward trend.
About 130 °C
About 130 °C would require an increase of 60 °C, larger than recent increments.
About 40 °C
About 40 °C would be below the boiling point of hexane, contradicting the trend.
About 100 °C
Correct: The increments per added carbon are shrinking (about 73, 47, 41, 37, 33 °C), so the next increment is roughly 30 °C: 69 + ~30 ≈ 100 °C.
qs.x: The increments per added carbon are shrinking (about 73, 47, 41, 37, 33 °C), so the next increment is roughly 30 °C: 69 + ~30 ≈ 100 °C. Trap: Extending the trend as if the increment per carbon were constant or growing rather than shrinking.

qs.q: Butanone boils about 44 °C higher than pentane despite the same molar mass. What is the best explanation?
o: Butanone has a permanent dipole from its polar C=O bond, adding dipole–dipole attractions to dispersion forces.
Correct: The polarized carbonyl group gives butanone a sizeable molecular dipole, so molecules attract each other beyond dispersion forces alone.
Butanone forms hydrogen bonds between carbonyl oxygens and C–H bonds as strongly as an alcohol does.
Butanone has no hydrogen bonded to an electronegative atom, so it cannot form strong hydrogen bonds with itself, and C–H···O interactions are weak.
Butanone has a much larger surface area than pentane.
Both molecules are four- to five-carbon chains of similar shape and surface area.
Butanone has more electrons than pentane, so its dispersion forces are far stronger.
The electron counts are nearly the same (butanone 40, pentane 42), so dispersion forces are similar.
qs.x: The polarized carbonyl group gives butanone a sizeable molecular dipole, so molecules attract each other beyond dispersion forces alone. Trap: Treating a carbonyl compound as a hydrogen-bond donor because it contains oxygen.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 8
text: A student analyzes an over-the-counter tablet mixture containing ibuprofen, aspirin, caffeine, and acetaminophen. Thin-layer chromatography (TLC) is run on silica gel plates with an ethyl acetate/hexane mobile phase. In 50% ethyl acetate, the solvent front traveled 8.0 cm, and the spot distances are in Table 1. Figure 1 shows the retention factor (Rf) of each compound as the percentage of ethyl acetate in the mobile phase changes. Silica gel is a polar stationary phase. In a separate experiment, the student extracts an aqueous caffeine solution with dichloromethane (DCM). The partition coefficient K for caffeine is 4.0, defined as the concentration in DCM divided by the concentration in water. To separate ibuprofen (a carboxylic acid with pKₐ ≈ 4.4) from caffeine, the student dissolves the mixture in diethyl ether and shakes it with aqueous sodium bicarbonate (pH ≈ 8.3), then separates the layers. The two layers are immiscible, and the student assumes that the extraction reaches equilibrium each time the layers are shaken together. Spots are visualized under ultraviolet light, since all four compounds absorb UV.

qs.q: In a repeat run with 50% ethyl acetate, the solvent front travels 10.0 cm. How far will the aspirin spot travel?
o: 4.0 cm
4.0 cm is the distance in the original run with an 8.0 cm solvent front.
6.3 cm
6.3 cm is 10.0 ÷ 1.6 and has no basis.
8.0 cm
8.0 cm is the original solvent front distance, not the spot distance.
5.0 cm
Correct: Rf depends on the system, not the plate length, so the distance is 0.50 × 10.0 cm = 5.0 cm.
qs.x: Rf depends on the system, not the plate length, so the distance is 0.50 × 10.0 cm = 5.0 cm. Trap: Assuming the spot distance stays fixed when the solvent front distance changes.

qs.q: Why does acetaminophen have the lowest Rf in Table 1?
o: It is the least polar, so it dissolves poorly in the mobile phase.
Nonpolar compounds interact weakly with silica and travel farther (higher Rf), as ibuprofen does.
It has the lowest molar mass and so diffuses the slowest.
Rf is governed by relative affinity for the phases, not by diffusion rate or molar mass alone.
It forms covalent bonds with the silica gel.
Adsorption to silica is by reversible noncovalent interactions, which is what makes chromatographic separation possible.
It is the most polar of the four compounds, so it adsorbs most strongly to the polar silica and is carried least by the mobile phase.
Correct: Compounds that hydrogen bond strongly (phenol and amide groups) interact with silica's surface and are retained.
qs.x: Compounds that hydrogen bond strongly (phenol and amide groups) interact with silica's surface and are retained. Trap: Thinking that polar compounds move farthest on a polar stationary phase.

qs.q: Which mobile phase composition in Figure 1 gives the greatest difference in Rf between aspirin and acetaminophen?
o: 50% ethyl acetate
20% ethyl acetate
At 20% the difference is only 0.20.
80% ethyl acetate
At 80% the difference is 0.25, smaller than at 50%.
The difference is identical at all three compositions.
The differences are 0.20, 0.30, and 0.25, so they are not identical.
qs.x: The Rf differences are 0.25 − 0.05 = 0.20 at 20%, 0.50 − 0.20 = 0.30 at 50%, and 0.70 − 0.45 = 0.25 at 80%. Trap: Choosing the composition where spots travel farthest rather than where they are most separated.

qs.q: After the ether solution is shaken with aqueous NaHCO₃, which species is found mainly in the aqueous layer?
o: Ibuprofen as its carboxylate anion
Correct: At pH 8.3 (well above pKₐ 4.4) ibuprofen is deprotonated to an ionic carboxylate that is water-soluble, while neutral caffeine stays in the ether.
Caffeine as its protonated cation
Caffeine is only a very weak base, so at pH 8.3 it is neutral and stays in the organic layer.
Ibuprofen in its neutral acid form
Neutral ibuprofen is more soluble in ether than in water, and the base converts it to its ionic form.
Both ibuprofen and caffeine in their neutral forms
Only the ionized species moves into water, so the two compounds are separated rather than remaining together.
qs.x: At pH 8.3 (well above pKₐ 4.4) ibuprofen is deprotonated to an ionic carboxylate that is water-soluble, while neutral caffeine stays in the ether. Trap: Forgetting that deprotonating an acid makes it ionic and water-soluble.

qs.q: A 100 mL aqueous caffeine solution is shaken once with 50 mL of DCM. What fraction of the caffeine is extracted into the DCM?
o: 80% is the result for equal volumes of the two solvents (K/(K + 1)).
50% would require K = 2.0 for these volumes, but K = 4.0 strongly favors DCM.
33% is the fraction left in the water, not the fraction extracted.
Correct: K = (n_DCM/50)/(n_aq/100) = 4.0, so n_DCM/n_aq = 2.0, and the fraction extracted is 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67.
qs.x: K = (n_DCM/50)/(n_aq/100) = 4.0, so n_DCM/n_aq = 2.0, and the fraction extracted is 2/(2 + 1) = 0.67. Trap: Ignoring the difference in volumes and using K/(K + 1), or reporting the fraction left behind.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 9
text: A student examines how the structure of an alkyl bromide affects its rate of nucleophilic substitution. In one set of experiments, each alkyl bromide reacts with sodium iodide in acetone, a polar aprotic solvent, under conditions that favor a bimolecular mechanism (SN2). In a second set, the same alkyl bromides are allowed to react with a solvent of aqueous ethanol (solvolysis), under conditions that favor a unimolecular mechanism (SN1). Approximate relative rates, set to 1 for the slowest measurable reaction in each series, are shown in Table 1. In addition, the student treats optically pure (R)-2-bromobutane with sodium iodide in acetone and analyzes the product with a polarimeter. A second experiment compares the rate of the reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane in acetone with the rate in water, a polar protic solvent. The student also plans to double the concentration of nucleophile in the solvolysis reaction of tert-butyl bromide. Throughout, the leaving group is bromide, and temperature is held constant. The student's goal is to connect each observation to the mechanism by which the reaction proceeds, and to the effects of substrate structure, solvent, and nucleophile on the rate.

qs.q: Why does tert-butyl bromide react so much faster than methyl bromide under SN1 conditions?
o: The tert-butyl carbon is less hindered, so the nucleophile attacks more easily.
The tertiary carbon is the most crowded, which is why it is slowest in SN2.
Bromide is a better leaving group from tertiary carbons because it is more basic there.
A better leaving group is a weaker base, and the leaving group is the same (Br⁻) in all cases.
The rate-determining step forms a tertiary carbocation, which is stabilized by electron donation from three alkyl groups.
Correct: In SN1 the slow step is ionization to a carbocation; alkyl groups stabilize the positive charge by hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary is fastest and methyl is slowest.
The tert-butyl group can donate a proton to the solvent, which accelerates the reaction.
The mechanism is carbocation formation and capture, not proton donation.
qs.x: In SN1 the slow step is ionization to a carbocation; alkyl groups stabilize the positive charge by hyperconjugation and induction, so tertiary is fastest and methyl is slowest. Trap: Reasoning from steric hindrance, which controls SN2, instead of carbocation stability for SN1.

qs.q: What is the major product of the reaction of (R)-2-bromobutane with NaI in acetone?
o: (R)-2-iodobutane
Retention would result from a double-inversion or front-side attack, which is not the SN2 mechanism.
A racemic mixture of 2-iodobutane
A racemic product is characteristic of SN1 through a planar carbocation, not SN2.
(S)-2-iodobutane
Correct: SN2 proceeds by backside attack and inversion of configuration. Iodide takes the same CIP priority position as bromine, so R becomes S.
(S)-2-iodobutane and 1-iodobutane in equal amounts
No rearrangement or substitution at C1 occurs; iodide substitutes at the carbon bearing the bromine.
qs.x: SN2 proceeds by backside attack and inversion of configuration. Iodide takes the same CIP priority position as bromine, so R becomes S. Trap: Predicting racemization for every substitution at a stereocenter, rather than inversion for SN2.

qs.q: How would the rate of the SN2 reaction of iodide with 1-bromobutane change when the solvent is changed from acetone to water?
o: It would increase, because water is more polar and stabilizes the transition state more.
Greater polarity helps SN1 ionization, but SN2 nucleophiles lose reactivity when strongly solvated.
It would increase, because water can donate protons to the nucleophile.
Protonation of the nucleophile would make it less nucleophilic.
It would decrease, because water hydrogen bonds to iodide and lowers its nucleophilicity.
Correct: Polar protic solvents solvate anions through hydrogen bonds, creating a shell that hinders attack; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile 'bare' and more reactive.
It would not change, because the substrate is the same.
Solvent strongly affects nucleophile reactivity even with the same substrate.
qs.x: Polar protic solvents solvate anions through hydrogen bonds, creating a shell that hinders attack; polar aprotic solvents leave the nucleophile 'bare' and more reactive. Trap: Assuming a more polar solvent always speeds substitution reactions.

qs.q: If the concentration of nucleophile is doubled in the solvolysis of tert-butyl bromide under SN1 conditions, how will the rate change?
o: It will double because the rate depends on both substrate and nucleophile.
A doubling would be seen for SN2, whose rate law is first order in each reactant.
It will not change appreciably, since the rate-determining step does not involve the nucleophile.
Correct: The SN1 rate law is rate = k[RBr]; ionization of the C–Br bond is slow, and the nucleophile attacks afterward in a fast step.
It will quadruple because the rate is second order in nucleophile.
There is no second-order dependence on nucleophile in either mechanism.
It will decrease because the added nucleophile competes with the solvent.
Added nucleophile does not slow ionization, which is the rate-determining step.
qs.x: The SN1 rate law is rate = k[RBr]; ionization of the C–Br bond is slow, and the nucleophile attacks afterward in a fast step. Trap: Applying the SN2 rate law, which includes nucleophile concentration, to an SN1 reaction.

passages.title: FL01 · Chem/Phys · Passage 10
text: A chemist studies the unimolecular isomerization of a compound in solution. The reaction is first order, and its rate constant k was measured at four temperatures, giving the data in Table 1. Figure 1 plots ln k against 1/T, where T is in kelvin, and the points fall on a straight line. The Arrhenius equation, k = A exp(−Ea/RT), describes the data, and R = 8.314 J/(mol·K). The overall reaction has ΔH° = −40 kJ/mol and ΔS° = −100 J/(mol·K), and both values are assumed to be independent of temperature over the range studied. In a second experiment, the chemist adds a catalyst that provides an alternative pathway for the same reaction, and she observes that the rate constant at 300 K increases substantially. The chemist reasons that the catalyst changes the kinetics of the reaction but not its thermodynamics. She also notes that the rate constant of a first-order reaction has units of inverse time, and that the half-life of such a reaction does not depend on the starting concentration. The same sample volume and solvent were used for all runs, and the temperature of each run was held constant by a thermostatted bath.

qs.q: The slope of the line in Figure 1 is approximately −7.2 × 10³ K. What is the activation energy of the reaction?
o: 7.2 kJ/mol
7.2 kJ/mol would result from ignoring R and converting units to kJ only.
0.87 kJ/mol
0.87 kJ/mol is the result of dividing by R rather than multiplying.
120 kJ/mol
120 kJ/mol is double the correct value and would come from an extra factor of 2 that is not in the Arrhenius relation.
60 kJ/mol
Correct: The slope equals −Ea/R, so Ea = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol = 60 kJ/mol.
qs.x: The slope equals −Ea/R, so Ea = (7.2 × 10³ K)(8.314 J/mol·K) = 6.0 × 10⁴ J/mol = 60 kJ/mol. Trap: Dividing the slope by R rather than multiplying by it, or forgetting that the slope is −Ea/R.

qs.q: What is the half-life of the compound at 320 K?
o: 222 s is 1/k, which omits the factor of ln 2.
Correct: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / (4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) = 154 s.
3.1 × 10⁻³ s is 0.693 × k, which multiplies instead of divides.
308 s is twice the correct half-life.
qs.x: For first-order kinetics, t½ = ln 2 / k = 0.693 / (4.50 × 10⁻³ s⁻¹) = 154 s. Trap: Using 1/k as the half-life and leaving out ln 2.

qs.q: How does the catalyst affect the reaction?
o: It lowers ΔG° of the reaction, making the products more stable.
ΔG° depends on the energies of reactants and products, which a catalyst does not change.
It lowers the activation energy and leaves ΔG° and the equilibrium constant unchanged.
Correct: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower Ea, speeding forward and reverse reactions equally, so K and the thermodynamic quantities (ΔH°, ΔG°) are unchanged.
It increases the equilibrium constant by increasing the forward rate only.
A catalyst accelerates the forward and reverse reactions equally, so K is not changed.
It raises the energy of the reactants so they are closer to the transition state.
A catalyst lowers the energy of the transition state relative to reactants; it does not raise the reactants' energy.
qs.x: A catalyst provides a pathway with lower Ea, speeding forward and reverse reactions equally, so K and the thermodynamic quantities (ΔH°, ΔG°) are unchanged. Trap: Believing a catalyst makes a reaction more spontaneous by changing ΔG°.

qs.q: What is ΔG° for the reaction at 300 K?
o: −10 kJ/mol
Correct: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −40 kJ/mol − (300 K)(−0.100 kJ/mol·K) = −40 + 30 = −10 kJ/mol.
−70 kJ/mol
−70 kJ/mol results from a sign error, −40 − 30.
+10 kJ/mol
+10 kJ/mol would result from reversing the sign of the whole calculation.
−30 kJ/mol
−30 kJ/mol would arise from using a different temperature or neglecting the 300 K factor.
qs.x: ΔG° = ΔH° − TΔS° = −40 kJ/mol − (300 K)(−0.100 kJ/mol·K) = −40 + 30 = −10 kJ/mol. Trap: Mishandling the sign of ΔS° or forgetting to convert J to kJ.

passages.title: FL01 · Psych/Soc · Passage 1
text: Researchers examined the effect of acute sleep restriction on working memory. 60 healthy adults aged 19 to 30 were randomly assigned to one of two groups. The control group slept 8 hours in the laboratory, and the restricted group was allowed only 4 hours. The next morning, each participant completed a computerized 2-back task, in which letters appear one at a time and the participant indicates whether the current letter matches the one shown two items earlier. Accuracy and mean reaction time on correct trials were recorded. The experimenters who scored the task did not know each participant's group, but participants knew how long they had been allowed to sleep. Group means were compared with independent-samples t-tests, using a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Results are shown in Table 1. In a separate sample of sleep-restricted adults, functional imaging showed reduced activation of the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex during the same task, relative to well-rested adults. The investigators concluded that a single night of short sleep impairs the ability to hold and update information over a few seconds.

qs.q: Random assignment of participants to the two sleep conditions primarily served to:
o: ensure that every participant would respond identically to the 2-back task regardless of sleep condition.
Individuals still differ in their sensitivity to sleep loss; randomization does not remove that variability.
make the results generalize to all adults regardless of age, sex, or baseline sleep habits.
Generalizability depends on how participants were sampled, not on how they were assigned.
eliminate the need for a statistical test of the group difference in 2-back accuracy.
Randomization does not remove chance differences, so a statistical test is still needed.
distribute pre-existing differences, such as baseline memory ability, roughly equally across groups.
Correct: Random assignment makes the groups comparable on average before treatment, so confounders are balanced by chance rather than by design.
qs.x: Random assignment makes the groups comparable on average before treatment, so confounders are balanced by chance rather than by design. Trap: Confusing random assignment (internal validity) with random sampling (external validity).

qs.q: Relative to the control group mean, the percent decrease in accuracy in the restricted group was closest to:
o: 8 is the absolute difference in percentage points, not a relative percent change.
This divides 8 by the restricted mean (76) rather than by the control baseline.
Correct: The difference is 84 − 76 = 8 percentage points; 8/84 = 0.095, or about 9.5% of the control value.
This value does not follow from either mean; 8/84 is about 0.095.
qs.x: The difference is 84 − 76 = 8 percentage points; 8/84 = 0.095, or about 9.5% of the control value. Trap: Dividing the difference by the wrong baseline (the experimental mean) or reporting percentage points as a percent change.

qs.q: The imaging finding in the sleep-restricted adults is most consistent with the idea that the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex:
o: encodes new declarative memories into long-term storage after a delay.
Long-term declarative encoding relies chiefly on the hippocampus and medial temporal lobe.
controls the release of cortisol and other hormones during stress.
Cortisol release is governed by the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis.
supports the maintenance and manipulation of information in working memory.
Correct: The DLPFC is a core region for executive function and working memory, so reduced activation fits poorer 2-back performance.
coordinates the timing and sequencing of voluntary movements of the limbs.
Movement timing is associated with the cerebellum and basal ganglia.
qs.x: The DLPFC is a core region for executive function and working memory, so reduced activation fits poorer 2-back performance. Trap: Attributing every memory deficit to the hippocampus when the task is short-term manipulation of information.

qs.q: Which feature of the design most weakens the conclusion that sleep loss alone caused the group difference in accuracy?
o: The scorers of the task did not know the group assignments of the participants.
Blind scoring reduces experimenter bias and is a strength.
Both groups completed the same 2-back task in the morning under identical conditions of testing.
Identical tasks and timing hold the testing conditions constant, which is a strength.
Participants knew their sleep condition, so expectations or effort could have differed between groups.
Correct: Participant awareness permits demand characteristics or motivational differences, a threat that cannot be fully blinded in a sleep manipulation.
Participants were randomly assigned to the sleep-deprived or the rested group before any testing began.
Random assignment strengthens causal inference.
qs.x: Participant awareness permits demand characteristics or motivational differences, a threat that cannot be fully blinded in a sleep manipulation. Trap: Choosing a design strength because it sounds technical when the question asks for a weakness.

qs.q: The reaction-time results in Table 1 indicate that the restricted group:
o: responded faster but less accurately, showing a speed-accuracy trade-off in the sleep-deprived group.
Faster responding would show a lower mean RT, but the restricted mean RT is higher.
was slower and less accurate, so the deficit is not a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Correct: Reaction time rose from 612 to 668 ms (p = 0.01) while accuracy fell, so the group was impaired on both measures.
showed no reliable difference from controls in either measure because the SDs are large.
The reported p = 0.01 is below 0.05, so the difference is statistically significant despite the SDs.
was more accurate on trials with longer reaction times, as expected for a speed-accuracy trade-off.
Table 1 reports group means only and says nothing about accuracy as a function of trial RT.
qs.x: Reaction time rose from 612 to 668 ms (p = 0.01) while accuracy fell, so the group was impaired on both measures. Trap: Assuming overlapping SDs automatically mean a non-significant result.
