questions.q: At pH 7.4, in a native gel electrophoresis experiment, a protein with an isoelectric point of 9.5 will most likely migrate toward:
o: the anode, because the protein has a net positive charge
positive molecules move toward the cathode, not the anode
the cathode, because the protein has a net negative charge
a negative protein would move toward the anode
neither electrode, because the net charge is zero
zero charge occurs only at pH = pI (9.5)
the cathode, because the protein has a net positive charge
Correct: A pH below the pI protonates the protein, giving a net positive charge, so it moves toward the negative electrode (cathode).
questions.x: A pH below the pI protonates the protein, giving a net positive charge, so it moves toward the negative electrode (cathode). Trap: Mixing up the direction of migration of cations and anions or misreading pH relative to pI.

questions.q: A purified antibody migrates at 150 kDa on SDS-PAGE without a reducing agent. With β-mercaptoethanol, bands are seen at 50 kDa and 25 kDa. These data are most consistent with an antibody composed of:
o: one 50 kDa and one 25 kDa chain linked by hydrogen bonds
one of each chain sums to 75 kDa, and SDS disrupts hydrogen bonds anyway
two heavy and two light chains linked by disulfide bonds
Correct: Reducing agents break disulfides: 2(50) + 2(25) = 150 kDa, so four chains are held together by disulfide bonds.
three 50 kDa chains linked by disulfide bonds
three 50 kDa chains would not produce a 25 kDa band and total 150 without light chains
one 150 kDa chain with internal peptide bonds cleaved
β-mercaptoethanol does not cleave peptide bonds
questions.x: Reducing agents break disulfides: 2(50) + 2(25) = 150 kDa, so four chains are held together by disulfide bonds. Trap: Ignoring that the two bands must sum to the total mass in the unreduced state.

questions.q: A template strand has the sequence 3'-TACGGATTC-5'. What is the sequence of the mRNA transcribed from it?
o: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'
Correct: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template and uses uracil: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'.
5'-UACGGAUUC-3'
this copies the template without complementing, and the polarity is wrong
3'-AUGCCUAAG-5'
this is complementary but the strand polarity is written backwards
5'-ATGCCTAAG-3'
mRNA contains uracil, not thymine
questions.x: mRNA is complementary and antiparallel to the template and uses uracil: 5'-AUGCCUAAG-3'. Trap: Writing the template sequence with T replaced by U instead of the complement.

questions.q: Cells lacking telomerase activity are cultured through many divisions. Which outcome is most likely?
o: Telomere lengthening through repeated lagging-strand synthesis at chromosome ends
lagging-strand synthesis causes the end-replication problem rather than lengthening
Loss of centromeres in daughter chromosomes, causing missegregation at anaphase
centromeres are not affected
Increase in Okazaki fragment length, which slows replication of the lagging strand
Okazaki fragment length is unrelated to telomerase
Progressive telomere shortening, eventually leading to senescence or apoptosis
Correct: DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of the lagging strand, so telomeres shorten each division unless telomerase extends them.
questions.x: DNA polymerase cannot fully replicate the 3' end of the lagging strand, so telomeres shorten each division unless telomerase extends them. Trap: Believing that lagging-strand synthesis maintains chromosome ends without telomerase.

questions.q: Three linked genes have recombination frequencies of 12% between A and B, 5% between B and C, and 7% between A and C. What is the gene order?
o: A-B-C
A-B-C would require A-C = 17
A-C-B
Correct: The largest distance (A-B = 12) is the sum of the other two (7 + 5), so C lies between A and B.
B-A-C
B-A-C would require B-C = 19
C-A-B
C-A-B would require C-B = 19, the sum of the other two distances
questions.x: The largest distance (A-B = 12) is the sum of the other two (7 + 5), so C lies between A and B. Trap: Ordering genes by the letters given instead of from the largest distance.

questions.q: In regions where malaria is endemic, the sickle cell allele remains at a substantial frequency in the population. Which concept best explains this?
o: Homozygotes for the sickle cell allele have the highest fitness
homozygous sickle cell individuals have severe disease
The allele is selectively neutral and maintained by genetic drift
strong, repeatable geographic patterns are not typical of drift
Heterozygotes have higher fitness than either homozygote
Correct: Heterozygotes are protected against severe malaria without sickle cell disease, maintaining both alleles (balancing selection).
The allele is maintained by repeated back mutation from the normal allele
mutation rates are too low to maintain the frequency
questions.x: Heterozygotes are protected against severe malaria without sickle cell disease, maintaining both alleles (balancing selection). Trap: Attributing high allele frequency to dominance or neutrality instead of selection.

questions.q: Which change would most likely increase the activity of phosphofructokinase-1 in a hepatocyte?
o: Increased fructose-2,6-bisphosphate
Correct: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, promoting glycolysis in the fed state.
Increased citrate
citrate signals abundant biosynthetic precursors and inhibits PFK-1
Increased ATP
high ATP is an allosteric inhibitor
Decreased AMP
AMP activates PFK-1, so a decrease would lower activity
questions.x: Fructose-2,6-bisphosphate is the most potent allosteric activator of PFK-1, promoting glycolysis in the fed state. Trap: Mistaking inhibitors for activators when the energy charge is considered.

questions.q: Complete β-oxidation of one molecule of palmitoyl-CoA (16 carbons) produces how many FADH₂?
o: 8 is the number of acetyl-CoA
15 is not related to the number of cycles
16 is the number of carbons
Correct: A 16-carbon fatty acid needs 7 cycles of β-oxidation, each producing one FADH₂ and one NADH, plus 8 acetyl-CoA.
questions.x: A 16-carbon fatty acid needs 7 cycles of β-oxidation, each producing one FADH₂ and one NADH, plus 8 acetyl-CoA. Trap: Equating the number of cycles to the number of acetyl-CoA produced.

questions.q: A mutation in the genes encoding claudins disrupts the tight junctions of an epithelium. Which defect would most likely result?
o: Increased paracellular leakage and loss of apical-basolateral protein segregation
Correct: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins separate.
Loss of the ability to anchor cells to the basal lamina through integrin-based contacts
hemidesmosomes anchor cells to the basal lamina
Loss of cytoplasmic communication between adjacent cells through connexin channels
gap junctions allow cytoplasmic communication
Loss of the keratin network inside cells, weakening their resistance to mechanical stress
keratin is a cytoplasmic intermediate filament and is not a claudin
questions.x: Tight junctions seal the space between cells and keep apical and basolateral proteins separate. Trap: Confusing the functions of tight junctions, gap junctions, and desmosomes.

questions.q: A drug blocks reverse transcriptase in cells infected with a retrovirus. Which step is directly prevented?
o: Synthesis of DNA from the viral RNA genome
Correct: Reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA, which is later integrated into the host genome.
Translation of viral proteins from viral RNA
translation uses host ribosomes and does not require reverse transcriptase
Assembly of virions at the plasma membrane
assembly occurs later and does not require reverse transcriptase
Entry of the virus by receptor-mediated endocytosis
entry occurs before reverse transcription
questions.x: Reverse transcriptase copies viral RNA into DNA, which is later integrated into the host genome. Trap: Assigning the enzyme to translation or assembly steps because they involve viral RNA.

questions.q: Nondisjunction of one homologous pair during meiosis I in a human spermatocyte would result in:
o: four gametes, none of which has the normal chromosome number for that pair
Correct: In meiosis I, homologs fail to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal, and all four gametes are n+1 or n-1 for that chromosome.
two normal gametes and two with an extra chromosome
two normal gametes arise only from meiosis II nondisjunction, which also gives one n+1 and one n-1 gamete, not two with extra copies
Two gametes with the normal number of chromosomes and two lacking that chromosome
an error in meiosis I affects both daughter cells, so two normal gametes cannot result
one abnormal gamete and three normal gametes
a single abnormal gamete does not match either meiotic division
questions.x: In meiosis I, homologs fail to separate, so both daughter cells are abnormal, and all four gametes are n+1 or n-1 for that chromosome. Trap: Confusing the outcomes of meiosis I and meiosis II nondisjunction.

questions.q: A cell with a loss-of-function mutation in TP53 experiences DNA damage. Compared with a normal cell, it is more likely to:
o: arrest in G1 so that the damage can be repaired
G1 arrest is caused by p53-induced p21
continue through the cell cycle without repair or apoptosis
Correct: p53 normally induces p21 and apoptotic genes after DNA damage; without it, checkpoints fail and mutations can be propagated.
undergo apoptosis through activation of caspases
apoptosis is promoted by p53
increase expression of the CDK inhibitor p21
p21 is a target of p53 and would not increase
questions.x: p53 normally induces p21 and apoptotic genes after DNA damage; without it, checkpoints fail and mutations can be propagated. Trap: Reversing the effect of a loss-of-function mutation in a tumor suppressor.

questions.q: Damage to the dorsal root of a spinal nerve would most likely cause:
o: loss of motor function in the corresponding region, with sensation preserved there
motor deficits result from ventral root damage
loss of both sensation and motor function in the corresponding region of the body
both roots are required to be damaged for loss of both
loss of the autonomic control of the heart and of voluntary movement in the arm
cardiac control uses cranial and sympathetic pathways, not this root
loss of sensation from the corresponding region with preserved motor function
Correct: Sensory neurons carry afferent signals into the cord through the dorsal root; motor neurons leave through the ventral root.
questions.x: Sensory neurons carry afferent signals into the cord through the dorsal root; motor neurons leave through the ventral root. Trap: Reversing the dorsal (sensory) and ventral (motor) roots.

questions.q: During intense exercise, hemoglobin in the muscle capillaries most likely shows:
o: increased oxygen affinity from increased CO₂ and H⁺, so less oxygen is released
higher CO₂ and H⁺ decrease hemoglobin affinity
decreased oxygen affinity from decreased temperature, so more oxygen is released
exercise increases, not decreases, temperature, and a lower temperature increases affinity
increased oxygen affinity from increased 2,3-BPG, so less oxygen is released
2,3-BPG increases release of oxygen by lowering affinity
decreased oxygen affinity from increased CO₂ and H⁺, releasing more oxygen
Correct: Lower pH, higher CO₂, and higher temperature shift the curve to the right (Bohr effect), favoring release of oxygen to tissue.
questions.x: Lower pH, higher CO₂, and higher temperature shift the curve to the right (Bohr effect), favoring release of oxygen to tissue. Trap: Shifting the curve in the wrong direction for the Bohr effect.

questions.q: Acidic chyme entering the duodenum stimulates the release of secretin, which acts on the pancreas to:
o: increase bicarbonate secretion to neutralize acid
Correct: Secretin from duodenal S cells promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which raises the duodenal pH.
increase secretion of pancreatic lipase only
lipase secretion is stimulated mainly by cholecystokinin
decrease secretion of bicarbonate
bicarbonate is increased, not decreased
stimulate release of gastric acid from parietal cells
gastrin, not secretin, stimulates gastric acid release
questions.x: Secretin from duodenal S cells promotes bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice, which raises the duodenal pH. Trap: Confusing the roles of secretin and cholecystokinin.

questions.q: A ball is thrown horizontally at 20 m/s from the edge of a 45 m cliff. Neglecting air resistance and using g = 10 m/s², how far from the base of the cliff does it land?
o: Correct: Fall time: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3 s. Horizontal distance = 20 m/s × 3 s = 60 m.
30 m uses a 1.5 s fall time, which corresponds to dropping 11 m rather than 45 m.
90 m would require a 4.5 s fall time (using h/g).
120 m comes from using t = 6 s, double the correct fall time.
questions.x: Fall time: 45 = ½(10)t², so t = 3 s. Horizontal distance = 20 m/s × 3 s = 60 m. Trap: Mixing up the fall-time formula, for example using t = h/g instead of √(2h/g).

questions.q: A 40 kg child sits 1.5 m from the pivot of a uniform seesaw. At what distance from the pivot on the other side must a 30 kg child sit to balance the seesaw?
o: Correct: At balance the torques are equal: 40(1.5) = 30d, so d = 2.0 m. The lighter child needs a longer lever arm.
1.1 m results from inverting the ratio (1.5 × 30/40).
1.5 m would only balance if the masses were equal.
3.0 m would be correct only if the mass ratio were 2:1.
questions.x: At balance the torques are equal: 40(1.5) = 30d, so d = 2.0 m. The lighter child needs a longer lever arm. Trap: Inverting the mass ratio so the lighter child sits closer to the pivot.

questions.q: What is the approximate absolute pressure at the bottom of a lake at a depth of 10 m? (Density of water = 1000 kg/m³, g = 9.8 m/s², atmospheric pressure = 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa)
o: 1.0 × 10⁵ Pa is only atmospheric pressure and ignores the water.
9.8 × 10⁴ Pa is the gauge pressure and omits the atmosphere.
3.0 × 10⁵ Pa would be reached at about 20 m depth.
questions.x: P = P_atm + ρgh = 1.0 × 10⁵ + (1000)(9.8)(10) = 1.0 × 10⁵ + 0.98 × 10⁵ ≈ 2.0 × 10⁵ Pa. Trap: Giving gauge pressure when absolute pressure is asked for.

questions.q: In the circuit, a 12 V battery is connected in series to a 4.0 Ω resistor, which is in series with a parallel combination of a 6.0 Ω resistor and a 3.0 Ω resistor. What is the current through the 6.0 Ω resistor?
o: 1.3 A is the current in the 3.0 Ω resistor (4.0/3.0).
2.0 A is the total current from the battery, which splits between the two parallel branches.
1.0 A would result from an equal split or wrong voltage.
Correct: The parallel pair equals (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 6.0 Ω and I = 2.0 A. The parallel pair has 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V across it, so I(6 Ω) = 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A.
questions.x: The parallel pair equals (6 × 3)/(6 + 3) = 2.0 Ω, so the total is 6.0 Ω and I = 2.0 A. The parallel pair has 2.0 A × 2.0 Ω = 4.0 V across it, so I(6 Ω) = 4.0/6.0 = 0.67 A. Trap: Giving the total current instead of the current in one parallel branch.

questions.q: A parallel-plate capacitor remains connected to a battery while the plate separation is doubled. What happens to the energy stored in the capacitor?
o: It doubles.
Doubling d does not increase C or U; capacitance falls when plates are farther apart.
It is reduced to one quarter of its original value.
A quarter would apply if both C and V were halved, but V is held fixed by the battery.
It is reduced to half its original value.
Correct: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling d halves C. With V fixed by the battery, U = ½CV² is halved.
It stays the same.
U depends on C, which changed.
questions.x: C = ε₀A/d, so doubling d halves C. With V fixed by the battery, U = ½CV² is halved. Trap: Assuming charge is fixed rather than voltage when the battery remains connected.

questions.q: An object is placed 30 cm from a converging lens with focal length 10 cm. Which describes the image?
o: Virtual, upright, and larger than the object
A virtual, upright, magnified image occurs only when the object is inside the focal length.
Real, inverted, and smaller than the object
Correct: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half the size.
Real, inverted, and the same size as the object
A same-size real image occurs when the object is at 2f (20 cm).
Virtual, upright, and smaller than the object
A converging lens makes virtual images only for objects inside f, and these are enlarged.
questions.x: 1/v = 1/10 − 1/30 = 1/15, so v = +15 cm (real, on the opposite side). Magnification = −15/30 = −0.5, so the image is inverted and half the size. Trap: Mixing up the 2f case (same size) with an object beyond 2f (smaller).

questions.q: A pipe closed at one end and open at the other has length 0.85 m. If the speed of sound is 340 m/s, what is the fundamental frequency?
o: 100 Hz
Correct: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and antinode at the open end, so λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz.
200 Hz
200 Hz is the fundamental of a pipe open at both ends (v/2L).
400 Hz
400 Hz is the fundamental if the wavelength were L.
50 Hz
50 Hz would apply to an 1.7 m pipe or λ = 2 × 3.4.
questions.x: A closed pipe has a node at the closed end and antinode at the open end, so λ = 4L = 3.4 m and f = 340/3.4 = 100 Hz. Trap: Using λ = 2L, which applies to a pipe open at both ends.

questions.q: Light of wavelength 400 nm strikes a metal with work function 2.0 eV. Use hc = 1240 eV·nm. What is the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons?
o: 2.0 eV
2.0 eV is the work function, the minimum energy needed to free an electron.
3.1 eV
3.1 eV is the total photon energy, not the kinetic energy left after overcoming the work function.
1.1 eV
Correct: The photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV, so KEmax = hf − φ = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV.
5.1 eV
5.1 eV adds the work function instead of subtracting it.
questions.x: The photon energy is 1240/400 = 3.1 eV, so KEmax = hf − φ = 3.1 − 2.0 = 1.1 eV. Trap: Adding the work function to the photon energy instead of subtracting it.

questions.q: The Kₛₚ of AgCl is 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰. What is the equilibrium concentration of Ag⁺ in a saturated solution of AgCl that is also 0.10 M in NaCl?
o: 1.3 × 10⁻⁵ M is the solubility in pure water (√Kₛₚ), without the common ion.
1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ M is Kₛₚ itself, not a concentration.
1.8 × 10⁻¹¹ M comes from dividing by 10 instead of dividing by 0.10.
Correct: [Ag⁺] = Kₛₚ/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common-ion effect.
questions.x: [Ag⁺] = Kₛₚ/[Cl⁻] = 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰ / 0.10 = 1.8 × 10⁻⁹ M, because of the common-ion effect. Trap: Using the pure-water solubility (square root of Kₛₚ) despite the common ion present.

questions.q: Carbon dioxide has polar C=O bonds, yet the CO₂ molecule is nonpolar. Which explains this?
o: The molecule is linear, so the two bond dipoles cancel.
Correct: VSEPR predicts linear geometry with two electron domains on carbon; the equal and opposite dipoles give a net dipole moment of zero.
The C=O bonds are actually nonpolar because carbon and oxygen have equal electronegativity.
Oxygen is significantly more electronegative than carbon, so each C=O bond is polar.
The molecule is bent, which gives dipoles that cancel.
A bent shape (like water or SO₂) leaves a net dipole.
Carbon dioxide has lone pairs on carbon that cancel the dipoles.
Carbon in CO₂ has no lone pairs.
questions.x: VSEPR predicts linear geometry with two electron domains on carbon; the equal and opposite dipoles give a net dipole moment of zero. Trap: Assuming that polar bonds always produce a polar molecule.

questions.q: In SDS-PAGE, a mixture of proteins of 15 kDa, 50 kDa, and 150 kDa is separated. Which statement is correct after the run?
o: The 15 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.

Correct: SDS coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their mass, so separation is determined by size: smaller proteins move through the gel matrix more easily and migrate farther toward the positive electrode.
The 150 kDa protein migrates farthest toward the anode.
Larger proteins are slowed more by the gel pores and so migrate less.
All three proteins migrate the same distance because SDS gives them equal charge.
Equal charge-to-mass ratio does not equalize migration; the gel acts as a sieve.
The proteins migrate toward the cathode, with the smallest protein moving most.
SDS-coated proteins are negatively charged and move to the anode (positive electrode).
questions.x: SDS coats proteins with negative charge in proportion to their mass, so separation is determined by size: smaller proteins move through the gel matrix more easily and migrate farther toward the positive electrode. Trap: Forgetting that SDS-coated proteins have similar charge density, so size alone determines mobility.

questions.q: Alanine is dissolved in a solution of pH 1.0. Which statement describes the predominant form of the amino acid?
o: It is a zwitterion with no net charge.
The zwitterion predominates near the isoelectric point (pH ≈ 6), not at pH 1.
The amino group is protonated and the carboxylate is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
At pH 1 the carboxyl is protonated, so the net charge cannot be −1.
Both the amino group and the carboxyl group are protonated, and the net charge is +1.
Correct: At pH well below the carboxyl pKₐ (~2.3), the COOH is protonated (neutral) and the amino group (pKₐ ~9.7) is protonated (+1), so the net charge is +1.
The amino group is neutral and the carboxylic acid is deprotonated, with net charge −1.
At low pH the amine is protonated, and the net charge is not negative.
questions.x: At pH well below the carboxyl pKₐ (~2.3), the COOH is protonated (neutral) and the amino group (pKₐ ~9.7) is protonated (+1), so the net charge is +1. Trap: Assuming the zwitterion is the dominant form at any pH.

questions.q: 1-Propanol is treated with pyridinium chlorochromate (PCC) in dichloromethane. What is the major organic product?
o: Propanoic acid
Propanoic acid would result from stronger aqueous oxidants such as chromic acid (Jones).
Propanal
Correct: PCC is a mild oxidant that, in anhydrous conditions, stops at the aldehyde stage for a primary alcohol.
Propanone
Propanone is the oxidation product of 2-propanol, a secondary alcohol.
Propene
PCC is not a dehydrating agent, so no alkene forms.
questions.x: PCC is a mild oxidant that, in anhydrous conditions, stops at the aldehyde stage for a primary alcohol. Trap: Over-oxidizing a primary alcohol to the carboxylic acid when a mild oxidant is used.

questions.q: Given C(s) + O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −394 kJ/mol, and CO(g) + ½O₂(g) → CO₂(g), ΔH = −283 kJ/mol, what is ΔH for C(s) + ½O₂(g) → CO(g)?
o: −111 kJ/mol
Correct: Reverse the second reaction (+283) and add it to the first (−394): −394 + 283 = −111 kJ/mol.
−677 kJ/mol
−677 kJ/mol adds both values without reversing the second equation.
+111 kJ/mol
+111 kJ/mol has the correct magnitude but the wrong sign.
−283 kJ/mol
−283 kJ/mol is the value for oxidizing CO to CO₂, not for forming CO.
questions.x: Reverse the second reaction (+283) and add it to the first (−394): −394 + 283 = −111 kJ/mol. Trap: Forgetting to reverse an equation (and flip the sign of ΔH) when applying Hess's law.

questions.q: The Haber process, N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g), is exothermic. What is the effect of increasing the temperature on the equilibrium constant K and the equilibrium yield of NH₃?
o: K increases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
K and yield rise with temperature for an endothermic reaction only.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
Correct: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts as a product, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. K, which depends only on temperature, decreases, and so does the NH₃ yield.
K is unchanged, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ decreases.
K is temperature dependent, so it changes when T changes.
K decreases, and the equilibrium yield of NH₃ increases.
K and the equilibrium composition are linked; a smaller K means less product, not more.
questions.x: For an exothermic reaction, heat acts as a product, so adding heat shifts the equilibrium toward reactants. K, which depends only on temperature, decreases, and so does the NH₃ yield. Trap: Thinking K is constant when temperature changes (only concentration changes leave K unchanged).

questions.q: A person rubs her elbow immediately after striking it, and the pain lessens. According to the gate control theory of pain, this occurs because:
o: rubbing destroys the nociceptors in the elbow so pain signals can no longer be generated or transmitted.
Nociceptors are not destroyed by rubbing; their signaling is modulated.
rubbing triggers release of cortisol, which blocks transmission along C fibers.
Cortisol release is a slow hormonal effect and does not explain immediate relief.
activation of large-diameter touch fibers excites inhibitory interneurons that reduce pain transmission in the spinal cord.
Correct: A-β touch input closes the 'gate' by activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, reducing relay of nociceptive signals.
touch fibers travel to the thalamus faster than pain fibers and cancel the pain signals in the cortex.
The gate operates in the spinal cord, before the thalamus and cortex.
questions.x: A-β touch input closes the 'gate' by activating inhibitory interneurons in the dorsal horn, reducing relay of nociceptive signals. Trap: Placing the pain-modulating mechanism in the brain instead of the dorsal horn of the spinal cord.

questions.q: In a signal detection experiment, an observer adopts a stricter criterion for reporting that a faint tone was present, while sensitivity does not change. Compared with before, the observer will have:
o: more hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
More of both occurs with a more lenient criterion.
fewer hits and more false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
The two rates move in the same direction when only the criterion shifts.
fewer hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Correct: A stricter criterion makes the observer say 'yes' less often, lowering both hits and false alarms without changing the sensitivity (d').
more hits and fewer false alarms, with no change in sensitivity.
Gaining hits while losing false alarms would require an increase in sensitivity.
questions.x: A stricter criterion makes the observer say 'yes' less often, lowering both hits and false alarms without changing the sensitivity (d'). Trap: Believing that criterion shifts trade hits for false alarms in opposite directions.

questions.q: A patient with bilateral hippocampal damage cannot recall meeting her doctor earlier in the day but improves from day to day on a mirror-tracing task without any memory of having practiced. These findings indicate that:
o: explicit and procedural memory share a single system located in the hippocampus and temporal lobes.
If one system served both, the skill learning would be lost.
procedural memory depends on systems other than those needed for new explicit memories.
Correct: Impaired explicit encoding with intact skill learning shows a dissociation: skills rely on basal ganglia and cerebellum.
the patient has retrograde amnesia only, with intact formation of new memories.
She cannot form new memories, which is anterograde amnesia; retrograde amnesia is loss of old memories.
procedural memories are stored in Wernicke's area and retrieved there.
Wernicke's area is a language comprehension region.
questions.x: Impaired explicit encoding with intact skill learning shows a dissociation: skills rely on basal ganglia and cerebellum. Trap: Assuming all memory types depend on the hippocampus.

questions.q: A 6-year-old watches water poured from a short, wide glass into a tall, thin glass and says that the tall glass now holds more water. According to Piaget, this child is most likely in the:
o: preoperational stage.
Correct: Failure to conserve volume because attention centers on one dimension (height) is typical of the preoperational stage.
sensorimotor stage.
The sensorimotor stage (birth to about age 2) involves object permanence.
concrete operational stage.
Concrete operational children understand conservation.
formal operational stage.
Formal operational thinking involves abstract hypothetical reasoning in adolescence.
questions.x: Failure to conserve volume because attention centers on one dimension (height) is typical of the preoperational stage. Trap: Assigning the stage by age alone without using the conservation clue.

questions.q: A man feels his heart pounding and his hands trembling after a near-collision, and he concludes that he must be afraid. This sequence is most consistent with:
o: the Cannon-Bard theory of emotion.
Cannon-Bard holds that arousal and emotional experience occur simultaneously and independently.
the Yerkes-Dodson law.
The Yerkes-Dodson law relates arousal to performance, not the origin of emotional experience.
the James-Lange theory of emotion.
Correct: James-Lange proposes that perception of bodily arousal produces the emotion; here arousal precedes the emotional labeling.
the opponent-process theory of emotion.
Opponent-process theory is about the aftereffects of emotional experiences, not their onset.
questions.x: James-Lange proposes that perception of bodily arousal produces the emotion; here arousal precedes the emotional labeling. Trap: Choosing the better-known multi-factor theory when the sequence described is simple arousal then feeling.

questions.q: In a twin study of a personality trait, the twin correlation is r = 0.50 for monozygotic pairs and r = 0.20 for dizygotic pairs. Using Falconer's formula, heritability = 2 × (r_MZ - r_DZ), the estimated heritability is:
o: 0.30 is the difference without the factor of 2.
0.70 is the sum of the two values, not the formula's difference.
1.00 would mean the trait is entirely genetic, which these data do not show.
questions.x: 2 × (0.50 − 0.20) = 2 × 0.30 = 0.60. Trap: Omitting the factor of 2 in Falconer's formula.

questions.q: A gambler keeps pulling a slot machine lever even though wins are unpredictable and sporadic. Which reinforcement schedule is operating, and why does it produce this pattern?
o: Fixed ratio, which yields a pause after each reinforcement and then a rapid burst of responding.
Slot machine wins are not tied to a fixed number of pulls.
Variable interval, which yields a slow and steady rate of responding with moderate extinction resistance.
Variable interval depends on time elapsed, not on number of responses.
Variable ratio, which yields a high and steady rate of responding that is resistant to extinction.
Correct: Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable ratio schedule, the most extinction-resistant schedule.
Fixed interval, which yields a scalloped pattern of responding that accelerates before reinforcement.
Fixed interval depends on elapsed time, and rates accelerate before the interval ends.
questions.x: Reinforcement after an unpredictable number of responses is a variable ratio schedule, the most extinction-resistant schedule. Trap: Matching the schedule by name rather than by whether it depends on responses or on time.

questions.q: A viewer who is not interested in the topic of an advertisement for a car is persuaded because the commercial features an attractive celebrity. According to the elaboration likelihood model, this is an example of:
o: the central route to persuasion, which relies on careful evaluation of the argument.
The central route involves careful evaluation of argument quality by a motivated listener.
cognitive dissonance reduction, in which attitudes change to match behavior.
Dissonance reduction involves changing attitudes to remove inconsistency with behavior.
the peripheral route to persuasion, which relies on superficial cues.
Correct: With low motivation, attitudes shift through superficial cues, such as source attractiveness, rather than argument quality.
the sleeper effect, in which a message persuades more after the source is forgotten.
The sleeper effect is persuasion rising over time as the source is forgotten.
questions.x: With low motivation, attitudes shift through superficial cues, such as source attractiveness, rather than argument quality. Trap: Calling a celebrity endorsement central because it is memorable.

questions.q: An experienced pianist plays a well-rehearsed piece. Her performance is likely to be best when she plays in front of a large audience, compared with when she is alone. This is an example of:
o: social facilitation, because an audience raises arousal and enhances well-learned tasks.
Correct: Audience presence raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, and for well-learned tasks this is correct, improving performance.
social loafing, because individual effort is reduced when people work together in groups.
Social loafing is reduced effort in a group when contributions are pooled, which is not the situation.
groupthink, because the audience suppresses dissent in favor of consensus.
Groupthink is a decision-making problem in cohesive groups.
deindividuation, because the audience provides anonymity and reduces self-awareness.
The pianist is identifiable to the audience, and deindividuation requires anonymity.
questions.x: Audience presence raises arousal, which strengthens the dominant response, and for well-learned tasks this is correct, improving performance. Trap: Predicting that an audience harms all performance, forgetting the task-difficulty qualifier.

questions.q: A teenager changes her goals and the way she dresses after noticing that her peers regard her as shy and unreliable. This is the best illustration of:
o: the self-serving bias.
The self-serving bias is attributing successes to the self and failures to external causes.
Cooley's looking-glass self.
Correct: The looking-glass self holds that self-concept is based on how we imagine others perceive and judge us.
the actual self matching the ideal self.
The scenario describes change prompted by others' views, with no stated match between actual and ideal self.
the spotlight effect.
The spotlight effect is overestimating how much others notice us, and not formation of the self-concept.
questions.x: The looking-glass self holds that self-concept is based on how we imagine others perceive and judge us. Trap: Choosing the self-concept term that sounds closest without matching the source of the change.

questions.q: A driver who is cut off in traffic concludes that the other driver is selfish and reckless. When the same person later cuts off another car, he explains that he was late for an important meeting. This pattern illustrates:
o: the self-serving bias exclusively, in which people credit successes to themselves and failures to others.
Self-serving bias concerns attributions after success and failure, not the differing explanations for actor and observer.
the actor-observer bias, including the fundamental attribution error when judging others.
Correct: He attributes others' behavior to disposition and his own to the situation, which is the actor-observer difference.
the just-world hypothesis, in which people believe outcomes are deserved.
The just-world hypothesis is the belief that people get what they deserve.
the halo effect, in which one positive trait colors judgments of other traits.
The halo effect is generalizing from one positive trait to other traits.
questions.x: He attributes others' behavior to disposition and his own to the situation, which is the actor-observer difference. Trap: Picking the self-serving bias because the person excuses his own behavior.

questions.q: A researcher recruits adults who volunteer for a new therapy program and compares them with adults who did not volunteer, finding that the volunteers have better outcomes at 6 months. The most serious threat to the validity of concluding that the therapy caused the improvement is:
o: a ceiling effect on all outcome measures, which compresses variability in the scores.
A ceiling effect is not suggested by the description.
observer drift in blinded raters, which gradually changes how outcomes are scored.
Observer drift is a measurement concern that is not described here.
selection bias, because volunteers may differ in motivation from non-volunteers.
Correct: Without random assignment, volunteers may differ systematically, which confounds the therapy effect.
the Hawthorne effect in the non-volunteer group, who changed behavior because they were observed.
The non-volunteers were not enrolled and cannot show a response to being observed.
questions.x: Without random assignment, volunteers may differ systematically, which confounds the therapy effect. Trap: Overlooking that self-selection into a condition prevents causal conclusions.

questions.q: In a country with a high birth rate that has begun to improve sanitation and medical care, death rates fall while birth rates remain high. According to the demographic transition model, the population will most likely:
o: grow rapidly.
Correct: Stage 2 features falling death rates with persistently high birth rates, so natural increase is large.
shrink rapidly.
Shrinkage occurs only if deaths exceed births, as in some late-stage populations.
remain stable.
Stability occurs when birth and death rates are both low and nearly equal (stage 4).
age rapidly with few children.
A rapidly aging population results when birth rates are low, which has not occurred.
questions.x: Stage 2 features falling death rates with persistently high birth rates, so natural increase is large. Trap: Confusing the early stage of the transition with the late stage.

questions.q: A study shows that Black women in the United States experience worse maternal outcomes than would be expected by considering race alone or gender alone. Which concept best describes the framework used to explain this?
o: Anomie, in which social norms fail to regulate behavior during rapid social change.
Anomie refers to normlessness.
Meritocracy, in which rewards are distributed according to individual effort.
Meritocracy is the idea that people are rewarded on merit and does not explain outcomes tied to identity.
Assimilation, in which a minority group adopts the dominant culture.
Assimilation is cultural adoption by minorities, not a theory of combined disadvantage.
Intersectionality, the overlap of social identities that yields distinct disadvantage.
Correct: Intersectionality holds that overlapping categories, such as race and gender, combine to produce unique forms of disadvantage.
questions.x: Intersectionality holds that overlapping categories, such as race and gender, combine to produce unique forms of disadvantage. Trap: Treating race and gender effects as simply additive.

questions.q: A sociologist studies how a group of hospital nurses and patients come to define a 'good patient' through their daily conversations, gestures, and labels. Which perspective is she using?
o: Functionalism, which views society as interdependent parts
Functionalism analyzes how social structures contribute to stability.
Conflict theory, which views society as competition over scarce resources
Conflict theory emphasizes power and competition among groups.
Symbolic interactionism
Correct: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how shared meanings are created and sustained through face-to-face interaction and symbols.
Rational choice theory, which views behavior as cost-benefit calculation
Rational choice theory assumes individuals weigh costs and benefits to maximize utility.
questions.x: Symbolic interactionism focuses on how shared meanings are created and sustained through face-to-face interaction and symbols. Trap: Using the macro-level theories for a micro-level interaction study.
